title: Rust Base Building Mechanics

text:
This deep-dive covers the structural rules of base building: how stability works, how building blocks are upgraded through tiers with the hammer, what building privilege allows and blocks, where you cannot place things, and how decay interacts with the structure. It goes below the overview in rust-building-raiding-foundation and leaves raid costs and turrets to rust-raiding-costs-defence and rust-turrets-deployables.

The headline is a sourcing gap. The privilege, placement and decay rules come from the Facepunch wiki Tool Cupboard page, which is undated, and the design of stability and upgrading comes from Facepunch devblogs dated 2014 to 2018. No Facepunch source obtained gives current stability percentages per piece, or current upgrade costs. Those figures appear only in a community guide. Confidence is Medium: the rules are primary-sourced but old, and the numeric stability and cost values are not primary-sourced.
title: Rust Base Building Mechanics

text:
- Stability is a structural-integrity system that makes unsupported buildings fall and prevents sky bridges; it does not account for weight, and unstable placements show a stability percentage (Devblog 35, 2014) [8].
- Stability was later moved onto entity links between building sockets, because the earlier physics-based method was slow and unreliable (Devblog 85, 2015) [9].
- Tier hitpoints were normalised in December 2017: Stone 500, Metal 1000, Armored 2000, with the Metal tier base cost raised from 150 to 200 metal fragments (Devblog 190) [6].
- The pillar building block was removed in February 2018, and wall frames were given the same stability as walls and doorways [7].
- The privilege radius is projected from the foundations connected to the Tool Cupboard, not from the cupboard itself [3].
- Unauthorised players can still place twig floors and wooden ladders inside someone's privilege; everything else is blocked [3].
- Default `decay.upkeep_grief_protection` and `decay.upkeep_period_minutes` are both 1440 minutes (24 hours) [4].
- The Livestock Update (1 October 2026) fixed upgrade-related door controller movement on high external gates and triangle foundation connections [1].

text:
- **Stability:** the structural-integrity value of a placed building piece, shown as a percentage on unstable placements [8].
- **Building block:** a placeable structural piece such as a foundation, wall, floor or roof, placed with the Building Plan [12].
- **Tier:** the material grade of a building block (twig, wood, stone, metal, armored) as used by the wiki decay list [3].
- **Entity links:** socket connections between entities, used by the stability system from 2015 [9].
- **Conditional model:** a piece model that appears only when neighbours are or are not connected, for example corners [10].
- **High external wall:** a tall freestanding wall that adds no upkeep and is protected from decay within a Tool Cupboard radius [3].
title: Rust Base Building Mechanics

text:
**Stability.** The system makes buildings fall down when they are unsupported. It lets players build self-supporting floors without a pillar or wall under every floor block, and it prevents sky bridges. The author said it would never be fully true to life, and weight is not considered [8]. Unstable placements show a stability percentage and the health bar background turns red [8]. In 2015 the calculation was converted from physics queries to entity links, where constructions track the state of their sockets and can refuse an attachment if a socket is occupied. The devblog says early results looked more robust but does not describe the new calculation [9]. Wall frames provide the same stability as walls and doorways since February 2018, and the post says they can be a useful way to add stability [7]. A community guide dated 11 June 2026 states that a piece at 0 percent collapses and that stability falls with distance from support, but it gives no thresholds and names no build [15].

**Tiers and upgrading.** Holding right-click with the hammer opens a menu for changing block type, rotating and demolishing; some options require Tool Cupboard influence [8]. Upgrading to stone or metal raises the block's maximum health where available [8]. The Facepunch wiki says the hammer is used to upgrade building materials and opens options on right-click, but it lists no upgrade paths or costs [13]. In December 2017 Facepunch normalised protection values: Armored 2000, Metal 1000, Stone 500, so metal is twice stone and armored twice metal [6]. The same post raised the metal tier base cost to 200 metal fragments from 150 and removed the small holes in the tiers [6]. The Building Plan costs 20 wood to craft; the wiki page itself does not describe tiers or stability [12]. A community guide says pieces are placed at twig and then upgraded, and that upgrading requires materials and building privilege [15].

**Conditional models and corners.** The 2014 building system infers corners where two edges intersect at 90 degrees, and foundation edge stones appear only when no connecting piece is present [10]. In 2015 conditional models were still client-side physics checks and could not change colliders [9].

**Building skins.** The 2014 plan was that walls could be upgraded from wood to stone and then metal [10]. The 2017 skin rework made it easier to define skinnable objects and replaceable materials [11]. In the Livestock Update, all four Ladder Hatch variants became skinnable through the workshop, and reskinning sheet metal doors no longer moves the attached door controller; upgrading high external gates likewise no longer moves it [1]. September 2026 added a per-item "random" skin option, and fixed random skins appearing on deployables [2].

**Building privilege radius.** The Tool Cupboard wiki says the radius is projected by the foundations connected to the cupboard, not from the cupboard's position, and that diagrams may not be to scale; the way to find the edge is to walk the base and watch for the privilege indicator [3]. Separate buildings need separate cupboards unless connected by foundations [3]. Placing a cupboard authorises its owner; authorised players can build, pick up deployables and trigger flame and shotgun traps [3]. The 2014 design had the same rule: only authorised players can use building tools within the radius [8].

**Placement restrictions.** In another player's privilege, unauthorised players may place twig floors and wooden ladders (orange "BUILDING BLOCKED" outline); any other placement shows red and sends a private chat notice [3]. High external walls do not add upkeep and do not decay inside the radius, and external cupboards can protect walls outside the main radius and stop players building just outside it [3]. Recent placement fixes: fireplaces cannot be deployed under a ceiling and rugs no longer block Workbench Upgrade placement [2]; storage adaptors cannot clip a head through a roof and drop boxes no longer allow a one-way peek [1].

**Decay and structure.** Without a cupboard holding resources, decay begins immediately. Once a material runs out, parts of that material decay on these timers: twig 1 hour, wood 3, stone 5, metal 8, armored 12, starting at the outermost exposed layers [3]. A destroyed cupboard holding resources consumes up to 24 hours of upkeep [3]. Walls, foundations, ceilings, roofs, doors and window pieces add to upkeep; items inside do not [3].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Check privilege coverage by walking the base, not by eye

- **Guidance:** After each expansion, walk the perimeter and confirm the privilege indicator is present at every external piece, adding a cupboard where it is not.
- **Evidence basis:** The radius is projected from connected foundations and the diagrams may not be to scale, and the wiki recommends this walk [3].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The page is official but undated.
- **So what:** Gaps in coverage let others build against your walls and leave pieces unprotected from decay.

## Guidance 2 — Plan stability with the hammer in hand and with wall frames, not pillars

- **Guidance:** Place pieces, read the stability percentage and use wall frames for extra support where needed.
- **Evidence basis:** Stability percentages are shown on unstable placements and wall frames match wall stability [7][8].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Both sources are from 2014 to 2018 and no current thresholds were obtained.
- **So what:** Do not rely on remembered span limits; test in the live build.

## Guidance 3 — Treat tier hitpoints and upgrade costs as unverified for 2026

- **Guidance:** Use the 2017 ratios (metal twice stone, armored twice metal) for planning but verify absolute values in game.
- **Evidence basis:** The ratios come from Devblog 190 and the community guide gives similar values with no build [6][15].
- **Confidence:** Low. The primary figures are nine years old and the later figures are community-only.
- **So what:** Do not publish guides quoting exact tier numbers without a fresh in-game check.

title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
This document gives an overview of how bases work in Rust: the Tool Cupboard (TC) and building privilege, upkeep and decay, doors and locks, a short tour of deployables, and the fundamentals of raiding with explosives and siege tools. It is a foundation: it explains the shape of the systems and points to deeper documents rather than listing every value.

The headline is that a base must be kept supplied through its TC or it decays, that the monthly updates keep changing the upkeep rules (a group upkeep tax arrived in September 2026), and that raid costs change with balance passes. Confidence is Medium: the mechanics come from the Facepunch wiki and devblogs, but the wiki's Tool Cupboard page is undated, hit-point tables were not obtainable from an openable source, and offline-raiding behaviour could not be sourced.
title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
- A Tool Cupboard costs 1000 wood to craft; without one a base decays and other players can build on it [2].
- Upkeep is a per-24-hour payment drawn from the TC inventory; with no resources in the TC, decay begins immediately [2].
- The wiki lists decay timers after the matching material runs out: twig 1 hour, wood 3 hours, stone 5 hours, metal 8 hours, armoured 12 hours (wiki page undated; check in game) [2].
- From the September 2026 update, TCs add a group upkeep tax: the first 4 players pay none, the next 6 add 2% each, later players 4% each, capped at 300% [3].
- Code locks use a four-digit code and cost 100 metal fragments; key locks cost 75 wood [4][5].
- A Timed Explosive Charge (C4) is crafted from 20 explosives, 5 cloth and 2 tech trash at Workbench Level 3 [6].
- The latest update checked, the Livestock Update (1 October 2026), made no upkeep change but fixed a battering ram bug that hit TCs through walls [1].
title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
- **Tool Cupboard (TC):** the deployable that grants building privilege and holds upkeep resources [2].
- **Building privilege:** authorisation to build and pick up deployables within the TC area [2].
- **Upkeep:** the periodic resource payment, a fraction of build cost, drawn from the TC [2].
- **Honeycomb:** multiple layers of walls placed to make raiding through that side more expensive [7].
- **Airlock:** two or more opposing doors within a single foundation [7].
- **Footprint:** the layout of a base's foundations [7].
title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
**Building privilege.** Placing a TC authorises the placer. Authorised players can build and pick up deployables in the radius and can set off flame and shotgun traps; others press E at the TC to authorise, and an authorised player can deauthorise by holding E. Anyone with access can hold E to clear every authorised player [2]. The privilege area is projected from the connected foundations, not from the TC position [2]. Unauthorised players can still place twig floors and wooden ladders, shown as an orange "BUILDING BLOCKED" outline; other placements show red [2]. Separate buildings each need their own TC coverage [2].

**Upkeep.** Upkeep is a per-24-hour payment, a fraction of the build cost, taken from the TC inventory. Walls, foundations, ceilings, roofs, doors and window pieces contribute; items inside the base such as sleeping bags do not. A stone base with sheet metal doors consumes only stone and metal fragments. Remaining protection time shows in the TC inventory [2]. High external walls add no upkeep and are protected within a TC's radius; small "external" TCs can cover walls outside the main radius [2].

**Decay.** Once a material runs out in the TC, parts made of it decay: twig after 1 hour, wood 3 hours, stone 5 hours, metal 8 hours, armoured 12 hours. Decay starts at the outermost exposed layers and works inward, and only parts of the exhausted material decay [2]. A destroyed TC holding resources consumes up to 24 hours of upkeep, protecting the base for 24 hours from that point [2].

**Group upkeep tax.** Since the September 2026 update, TCs add an upkeep tax based on the number of players in the base. Counted players are those authorised on the TC or a code lock (guest codes included) plus those deauthorised from either in the last 24 hours. Server owners can adjust or disable it through ConVars in the Decay class [3].

**Doors and locks.** The code lock opens with a four-digit code [4]. The key lock is placed on a door and keys can be shared with friends [5]. The armoured door is described as an extremely strong door with a hatch to see and shoot out of [8]. Doors are one input to base design alongside honeycomb and airlock layouts [7].

**Deployables overview.** The Facepunch wiki groups base-related items as doors and locks, barricades, walls and windows, and raiding tools [9]. The Livestock Update added animal gates and fences and allowed Smart Alarms to sit on other deployables [1]. The Tin Can Alarm can be rigged with grenades and similar items, and the Mortar was added as a raiding and anti-personnel deployable in May 2026 [10].

**Raiding fundamentals.** The wiki lists the satchel charge, timed explosive charge, explosives, beancan and F1 grenades, battering ram, siege tower, catapult and cannon as raiding items [9]. The satchel charge is described as useful for destroying wood and sheet metal doors [11]. The battering ram is a siege weapon for breaking through wooden and stone structures and must be repaired with high quality metal to keep functioning [12]. The Mortar fires shells of two types, one aimed at players and one at structures, fired without a visual guide [10]. Parts of a base whose TC has run dry decay on the timers above, which makes neglected bases weaker targets [2].

**Offline considerations.** The Tool Cupboard wiki page does not address offline behaviour [2]. Upkeep is a per-24-hour payment drawn from the TC, so stocked resources are what protect a base from decay; the page does not tie this to whether owners are online [2]. No Facepunch source on offline raid protection was opened for this document; see Open Questions.
title: Rust Building and Raiding: Foundation

text:
## Guidance 1 — Keep the TC stocked for the material that decays first

- **Guidance:** Stock the TC with more than enough of every material your base uses, prioritising the lowest tier present, because each tier begins to decay on its own timer once its material runs out.
- **Evidence basis:** Upkeep is drawn from the TC and the per-tier decay timers are documented [2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The wiki page is official but undated, and the upkeep rules changed in September 2026 [3].
- **So what:** Check the TC protection timer in game after each monthly update rather than trusting remembered numbers.

## Guidance 2 — Budget for the group upkeep tax before adding teammates

- **Guidance:** Keep the authorised and code-lock player count low, and remove stale guest codes, to avoid a larger upkeep bill.
- **Evidence basis:** The tax is based on players authorised on the TC or a code lock plus those deauthorised in the last 24 hours [3].
- **Confidence:** High. This comes directly from the Facepunch devblog, though server owners may change it [3].
- **So what:** On an unfamiliar server, ask whether the Decay ConVars were changed.

## Guidance 3 — Expect raid costs to drift and verify before planning

- **Guidance:** Use the wiki crafting costs only as a starting point; recheck explosives and tool costs each patch.
- **Evidence basis:** Explosive costs are documented per item [6][11][12], and raid-related items and fixes changed repeatedly in recent updates [1][3][10].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Costs are cited, but the wiki is undated and damage values were not obtained.
- **So what:** Do not plan a raid from a months-old guide.

title: Rust Raiding Costs and Base Defence

text:
This deep-dive goes below the foundation document into what it costs to break a base and what defends one: structure and door hit points by tier, explosive damage and sulfur cost, how many explosives each wall or door takes, the upkeep rules that keep a base alive, and the protections that exist in vanilla Rust. The only vanilla protection found in Facepunch sources is the Softcore raid window and TC raid-blocking system added in July 2026 [3], plus the upkeep grace after a TC is destroyed [5].

Confidence is Low. The Facepunch wiki item pages do not list hit points or damage [6][7][8], so the numeric tables come from third-party raid charts that say they were derived from server files or live game data [10][11][12] and that disagree with each other in places. Anything that disagrees is shown side by side and also listed in Open Questions.
title: Rust Raiding Costs and Base Defence

text:
- From a third-party table said to come from the 22 September 2026 server files: wood wall 250 HP, stone 500, sheet metal 1,000, armoured 2,000 [10].
- The same source gives C4 as 550 explosion damage, rocket as 275 explosion plus 75 blunt, and satchel as 75 explosion plus 200 blunt plus 200 stab [10].
- Sulfur to craft: C4 2,200, rocket 1,400, satchel 480; three independent third-party pages agree [10][11][12].
- Third-party charts put a stone wall at 2 C4 (about 4,400 sulfur) and a sheet metal wall at 4 C4 (8,800 sulfur) from the hard side [10][11].
- C4 crafts from 20 explosives, 5 cloth and 2 tech trash at Workbench Level 3 [6]; the satchel from 4 beancan grenades, 1 rope and 1 small stash at Workbench Level 1 [8].
- Facepunch's wiki gives decay timers after upkeep runs out (twig 1 hour to armoured 12 hours), and a destroyed TC burns up to 24 hours of upkeep to hold a base for 24 hours [5].
- Since 2 July 2026, Softcore servers default to raids only 6 PM to 9 PM server time, and a TC at least 1 hour old blocks raids on walls, floors, roofs, doors and ladder hatches outside that window [3].
- No vanilla offline-raid protection was found in Facepunch sources; offline protection on normal servers appears only as plugins [14] *(assessed from absence of evidence)*.

text:
- **Hard side / soft side:** the outer face of a wall or door versus the interior-facing face, which takes less explosive damage; the soft side is described as the face with the X-shaped braces [10].
- **Raid cost (sulfur):** the raw sulfur needed to craft the explosives used, a standard way third parties compare options [10][11].
- **Honeycomb:** layered walls that multiply the cost of raiding through one side [11].
- **Softcore raid window:** a scheduled period in which raiding is allowed on Softcore servers [3].
- **Group upkeep tax:** the player-count based surcharge on TC upkeep [2].
title: Rust Raiding Costs and Base Defence

text:
**Why counts are not simple division.** C4 is listed at 550 explosion damage but a 500 HP stone wall is listed as needing 2 C4 [10]. The source does not explain the gap; damage falls off with distance, with C4 at full damage at 0 m and zero at 4 m [10]. Treat the per-target counts as the figure to use and the damage numbers as context [10].

**Explosive damage.** The listed profiles are C4 550 explosion; rocket 275 explosion and 75 blunt (full at 1 m, zero at 3.8 m); satchel 75 explosion, 200 blunt and 200 stab; beancan 15 explosion, 50 blunt and 50 stab [10]. The Facepunch wiki pages for C4, satchel and the armoured door do not publish damage or HP; they give recipes, recycling and loot sources only [6][7][8].

**Soft side.** The interior face takes less damage, so fewer explosives are needed. One source gives beancans on a stone wall as 46 from the soft side instead of 64 [10]; another says the soft side takes "roughly half" the explosives without counts [11]. Most calculators default to the hard side [11].

**Weakest-path principle.** Per the charts, the cheapest breach point sets a base's real cost. A sheet metal wall is listed at 4 C4 and a sheet metal door at 1 C4 [10]. A wooden door can be defeated by fire or melee, or one satchel [11].

**Upkeep.** The TC draws a fraction of build cost every 24 hours; the wiki gives no percentages [5]. A 2017 devblog set the fraction by base size (10% for 1 to 15 blocks, up to 33% above 75 blocks) and made it convar-configurable [4]. The September 2026 group tax adds 2% per player for players 5 to 10 and 4% each beyond, capped at 300% [2]. Treat the 2017 percentages as historical only [4]. The Power Trip update (6 August 2026) gave high external walls a static 20% upkeep, described as the middle of the building-block range of 10% to 33%, so the 2017 band endpoints are still the range Facepunch cites in 2026 [9]. The Breach and Clear text says the group tax is adjustable or disableable through convars in the Decay class, with no names given [2]. No Facepunch source gives upkeep fractions per tier or piece.

**Decay and grief protection.** After a material runs out in the TC, parts made of it decay on the timers in Reference Data [5]. A destroyed TC holding resources eats up to 24 hours of upkeep so the base does not decay for 24 hours, designed so a raided player does not lose their base [5]. Raiders can take over the base with their own doors [5].

**Softcore raid windows and raid blocking.** In the Common Ground update (2 July 2026), Softcore raids default to 6 PM to 9 PM server local time. Outside windows, a TC projects a raid-blocking system covering players inside its radius: walls, floors, roofs, doors and ladder hatches cannot be raided. Deployables and an unprotected TC can still be attacked, and the TC must be at least 1 hour old [3]. A third party adds that outside the window explosive and projectile damage on core building parts is blocked while twig, high external walls and gates, and melee stay vulnerable [10]; this was not confirmed against Facepunch text.

**Offline raiding on normal servers.** The Tool Cupboard wiki page does not use the term [5]. Offline protection appears as server plugins: one limits the number of offline raids per player or team per day and per wipe [14]. That is configuration of individual servers, not a vanilla rule [14].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Make the cheapest entry point as expensive as the walls

- **Guidance:** Put your best door tier and any airlock on the shortest path to the TC rather than adding wall layers elsewhere.
- **Evidence basis:** A sheet metal door is listed at 1 C4 while a sheet metal wall is 4, and a honeycomb of three stone layers is 6 C4 [10][11].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The relative counts agree across two charts, but absolute numbers are third-party.
- **So what:** Spend resources on the weakest link first.

## Guidance 2 — Keep the TC stocked and expect it to be targeted

- **Guidance:** Keep upkeep resources in the TC and expect raiders to look for it; a destroyed TC still buys a day of decay protection.
- **Evidence basis:** The Facepunch wiki describes the 24-hour grace and that raiders look for the TC [5].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Official page, but undated.
- **So what:** Do not rely on the 24-hour grace to survive an absence; restock after a raid.

## Guidance 3 — On vanilla servers, plan for no offline protection

- **Guidance:** Assume no offline protection unless the server advertises Softcore or a plugin.
- **Evidence basis:** No vanilla offline mechanism was found; only plugins and Softcore windows appear in sources [3][14].
- **Confidence:** Low. This rests on absence of evidence and community plugin pages.
- **So what:** Check server rules and tags before committing to a base location.

## Guidance 4 — Verify counts against the current build before a raid

- **Guidance:** Treat all numbers here as approximations and check an up-to-date calculator or an in-game test.
- **Evidence basis:** Two charts conflict and the Facepunch wiki gives no HP [7][10][11].
- **Confidence:** High. The conflict is directly visible in the cited sources.
- **So what:** Do not budget a raid from a stale chart.

title: Rust Turrets and Defensive Deployables

text:
This deep-dive covers the defensive deployables that sit on top of the base layer described in the foundation document: the auto turret, shotgun trap, flame turret, SAM site, snap trap, landmine, floor spikes, the barricade family, the two alarms and the two lock types. For each it records crafting cost, workbench level, power draw and ammunition where the Facepunch wiki gives them, and the recent patch changes that touched them. Raid costs and structure hit points are left to rust-raiding-costs-defence.

The headline is that the Facepunch item pages give recipes and some power figures but no range, health or damage for any of these items, so those values are listed as unsourced rather than guessed. Confidence is Medium: recipes, power figures and patch history are primary and tied to the checked build, but targeting behaviour, ammo capacities and the SAM site's roles come from a single community guide that states no game version.
title: Rust Turrets and Defensive Deployables

text:
- The auto turret costs 10 high quality metal, 1 CCTV camera and 1 targeting computer at Workbench Level 2, draws 10 rW, and searches a 180-degree arc facing the player who placed it [7].
- The shotgun trap costs 500 wood, 250 metal fragments, 2 gears and 2 rope at Workbench Level 1 and is loaded with handmade shells [8].
- The flame turret costs 200 metal fragments, 2 empty propane tanks and 1 gears at Workbench Level 1 and requires low grade fuel [9].
- The wiki lists the SAM site as not craftable, drawing 25 rW and using SAM ammo [10][11].
- A Tool Cupboard authorises its owner for flame and shotgun traps; the wiki words this as traps "that require TC privilege" [25].
- The September 2026 update made SAM sites better at shooting down hostile drones [2]; the October 2026 Livestock Update let remotely controlled turrets hit reactive targets and overhauled sandbag barricades [1].
- No item page opened for this document lists range, health or damage for a turret, trap or barricade [7][8][9][10][13][14][15][18][19][20].

text:

Power and ammo are given only where a source states them.

Not covered: explosive costs and structure HP (see rust-raiding-costs-defence), the electrical circuit system in general (see rust-electricity-logic), weapon and ammo stats (see rust-weapons-ammo), wildlife and NPC turrets (see rust-wildlife-npcs) and plugin behaviour on modded servers. title: Rust Turrets and Defensive Deployables

text:
- **rW:** the unit the wiki uses for power draw on an item's electrical section [7][10][22].
- **Building privilege (TC privilege):** authorisation granted through a Tool Cupboard, which the wiki ties to flame and shotgun traps [25].
- **Peacekeeper / Attack All:** the two auto turret targeting modes as described by one community guide (green and red laser) [26].
title: Rust Turrets and Defensive Deployables

text:
**Auto turret.** The wiki describes it as an item that engages moving targets it has line of sight to, requiring a projectile weapon and matching ammunition. It draws 10 rW and has outputs for Has Target, Low Ammo and No Ammo. It searches a 180-degree arc facing the player at placement [7]. A community guide adds that the turret does not read the Tool Cupboard, so each turret is authorised individually, and that Peacekeeper mode treats everyone as friendly until they act hostile while Attack All fires at anyone unauthorised; it also says settings need building privilege and the turret powered off [26]. That guide gives no game version [26]. Patch notes show turrets attached to a burst-fire gun (the M16A2) use burst fire since 2 July 2026 [3], and a fix stopped turrets hitting a player's shield after it broke on 4 June 2026 [4].

**Shotgun trap.** A trap triggered by movement, placed near doorways and loaded with handmade shells [8]. Handmade shells are listed as ammo with multiple projectiles [12]. The Tool Cupboard wiki says authorisation covers traps that require TC privilege, naming flame and shotgun traps [25]. The community guide says the trap fires at unauthorised players when a TC is in range and at everyone otherwise, needs no power, and cites roughly two shells per second and a 384-shell reserve as commonly quoted figures; none of that is on the wiki item page [26].

**Flame turret.** The wiki describes an automated turret that requires low grade fuel and sprays flames when triggered [9]. The community guide states a fuel capacity of up to 500, a roughly 90-degree frontal cone, and that it needs no power [26]. The wiki page gives no fuel use, range or damage [9].

**SAM site.** Requires 25 electricity, takes power in and passes the remainder through, uses SAM ammo, and has Has Target, Low Ammo and No Ammo outputs plus an Invert Mode input [10]. The SAM ammo page says the missile "contains a rudimentary guidance system" [11]. The community guide describes an attacker mode against unauthorised player-piloted air vehicles and a defender mode against MLRS rockets, and says about three sites are needed against a 12-rocket barrage [26]. September 2026 notes say the site is now much better at destroying hostile drones [2].

**Ground traps.** The snap trap is a metal trap that can injure or kill when stepped on and can be picked up after triggering [18]. The landmine can be disarmed by a friend if you stand on it [19]. Wooden floor spikes slow and hurt anyone walking over them [20]. None of the three pages lists a damage value [18][19][20].

**Barricades.** The wooden barricade hurts players and animals that run into it [13]. The barbed wooden barricade and the metal barricade both damage and slow players [15][16]. The stone and sandbag barricades are described as protective barricades [14][17]. The Livestock Update overhauled sandbags into a stackable deployable with a lower crafting cost, and sandbag barricades found in loot now come as a stack of 4 [1]. No page lists barricade health [13][14][15][16][17].

**Alarms.** The tin can alarm clatters loudly when disturbed [21]; in May 2026 it became riggable with explosives and similar items [5]. The smart alarm sends a phone notification when powered, draws 1 rW and passes power through [22]; since October 2026 it can be placed on top of other deployables [1].

**Locks.** The code lock is "an electronic lock" opened by a four-digit code [23]. The key lock is placed on a door and a key can be crafted for friends [24]. Players authorised on a code lock, including guest-code access, count toward the group upkeep tax for the base [2].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Treat turret and trap ranges and damage as unknown until tested on the live build

- **Guidance:** Do not plan a defence around range, damage or health numbers quoted from memory or videos; test placement and coverage on the current update.
- **Evidence basis:** None of the Facepunch item pages for the turret, traps, SAM site or barricades states those values [7][8][9][10][13], and turret behaviour was patched in three recent updates [2][3][4].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The absence is verified on the pages opened, but the values may exist in game data not checked.
- **So what:** Budget time for in-game testing after each monthly update.

## Guidance 2 — Verify authorisation on each turret separately

- **Guidance:** After placing auto turrets, check each one's authorisation list rather than assuming the TC covers it.
- **Evidence basis:** A community guide says turrets do not read the TC [26]; the wiki's TC authorisation text names only flame and shotgun traps [25]; a May 2026 fix concerned authorising a friend at a TC or turret [5].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The turret claim rests on one undated community guide.
- **So what:** A teammate missing from a turret list is a likely cause of friendly-fire incidents.

## Guidance 3 — Count power headroom before wiring turrets and a SAM site on one supply

- **Guidance:** Add the draws (10 rW per auto turret, 25 rW for a SAM site, 1 rW per smart alarm) before choosing a generator and battery setup.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki lists those draws [7][10][22].
- **Confidence:** High. The figures are on Facepunch pages for the checked build; the wiring design itself is not covered here.
- **So what:** An under-supplied circuit leaves defences unpowered.

title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text:
This deep-dive extends the survival overview in rust-game-mechanics-foundation by explaining how damage is dealt and reduced in Rust: per-ammunition base damage and headshot multipliers, how clothing and armour reduce damage by damage type and body area, how melee compares with ranged fire, how bleeding is generated and treated, and what is and is not sourced for explosions and falls. Values were read from the Facepunch Rust Wiki item pages on 2026-10-08, when the Livestock Update (1 October 2026) was the latest update [1].

Document confidence is Medium. Per-item numbers come from Facepunch's own wiki, but the wiki pages omit several mechanics: there is no sourced hit-zone table beyond the headshot multiplier, no sourced fall-damage formula, and no sourced explosion damage numbers. The bleeding formula comes from a single community article that states no build [18]. Those gaps are listed in Open Questions rather than filled from memory.
title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text:
- The Facepunch wiki lists a headshot multiplier of x2 for 5.56 rifle ammunition, pistol ammunition and the Salvaged Sword, x1.5 for Hunting Bow arrows, and x1 to x2 for shotgun ammunition depending on type (checked against the Livestock Update) [3][6][7][8][9].
- Clothing lists the body parts it protects, and damage is reduced according to which body part was hit; clothing does not change hitbox size [2].
- Protection is expressed per damage type: the Metal Facemask lists Projectile 50%, Melee 70% and Explosion 50% for the head slot only [11], and the Hazmat Suit lists 30% projectile, 30% melee and 30% explosion across the full body [13].
- Some clothing has negative protection: the Road Sign Jacket lists Cold -34% [12].
- The Bandage lists Bleeding -50 and Instant Health +5 [14].
- The Livestock Update lists no change to bleeding or fall damage; it did raise the Water Wheel's melee protection and change attack-helicopter armour plates [1].
- No Facepunch source opened for this document gives a fall-damage formula or explosion damage numbers *(assessed from the pages checked; see Open Questions)*.
title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text: Covered: player-versus-player and player-versus-NPC damage on vanilla PC servers: headshot multipliers, protection values of selected clothing and armour, melee versus ranged stats, bleeding, and what is known about explosive and fall damage. Not covered: weapon-by-weapon rankings and attachments (see rust-weapons-ammo), structure damage and raid costs (see rust-raiding-costs-defence), and server convars that change damage (see rust-server-convars-reference). Modded servers and console are excluded. Facts were checked against the Livestock Update (1 October 2026).
title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text:
- **Headshot multiplier:** the factor listed on a weapon's wiki page for head hits [3].
- **Protection:** a per-damage-type percentage listed on a clothing item page [11][12][13].
- **Hit area:** the body part struck, determined by a player collision mesh that does not change with clothing [2].
- **Bleeding:** a status value that causes damage over time [18].
- **Slot and layer:** a clothing item occupies a body slot on the Clothing or Armor layer, for example the Metal Facemask in the Head slot on both layers [11].
title: Rust Combat and Damage Model

text:
**Evidence layer.** The hit-area design is from a Facepunch devblog written before the current build, so it is cited as design intent; the numbers come from current wiki pages.

**Hit areas and clothing.** Devblog 117 describes the replacement of mesh-based hitboxes. Previously the exact player model and clothing meshes were colliders, so metal hits did less damage than skin or cloth and results were effectively random in firefights. Under the new system clothing lists the body parts it protects, damage is reduced based on which body part was hit, gloves can add to overall protection, and the struck body part comes from a player collision mesh that does not change with clothing [2]. The same post says per-weapon body-part multipliers were being added, giving the example of higher headshot multipliers for sniper rifles and lower ones for shotguns, and that the direction was undecided [2]. The current wiki headshot values differ by weapon, which is consistent with that design [3][7][8].

**Ranged damage.** The wiki lists damage per ammunition type on each weapon page, with a headshot multiplier. On the Assault Rifle, 5.56 Rifle Ammo, HV and Explosive list 50 damage and Incendiary lists 56, all with x2 [3]. On the Bolt Action Rifle and L96 pages the same four 5.56 types list 80 damage (89.6 Incendiary) with x2 [4][5]. On the Thompson, Pistol Bullet and HV Pistol Ammo list 37.5 and Incendiary lists 42, with x2 [6]. On the Pump Shotgun, 12 Gauge Slug lists 80 with x2, Buckshot 15 with x1.2, Incendiary Shell 15 with x1 and Handmade Shell 9 with x1.2; the page gives no pellet count, so a per-shot total cannot be derived from the wiki [7]. Hunting Bow arrows list Wooden 50, Bone 40, Fire 40 and High Velocity 40, all with x1.5 [8].

**Weapon modifiers.** The Assault Rifle page lists attachment effects: Gas Compression Overdrive (Damage +20%), Military Silencer (Damage -25%), Oil Filter Silencer and Soda Can Silencer (Damage -30%), and Muzzle Brake (Damage -15%) [3].

**Melee.** The Salvaged Sword lists Damage Total 50, Attack Rate 0.8, Headshot Multiplier 2, Range Max 1.5 and Attack Radius 0.3 [9]. The Stone Pickaxe lists Damage Total 17, Attack Rate 1.1, Headshot Multiplier 2, Range Max 1.5 and Attack Radius 0.3 [10]. Both pages also list gather figures against Flesh (Gather Damage 10) [9][10]; the pages do not explain how these relate to combat damage, so they are not interpreted here.

**Protection by damage type.** Clothing pages list percentages per damage type. Metal Facemask: Projectile 50%, Melee 70%, Bite 8%, Cold -4%, Explosion 50%, head only [11]. Road Sign Jacket: Projectile 20%, Melee 20%, Bite 40%, Cold -34%, chest on the Armor layer [12]. Hazmat Suit: Projectile 30%, Melee 30%, Bite 50%, Radiation 50%, Cold 50%, Explosion 30%, full body [13]. The pages opened do not state how multiple items combine, so stacking is not asserted here.

**Bleeding.** The Facepunch wiki lists the Bandage as Bleeding -50, Instant Health +5, Poison -2, and describes it only as healing yourself or a target [14]. A community article states that bleeding equals 20% of damage dealt, ticking 1 damage every 6 seconds until the total is applied, and that bandages or syringes stop it immediately; it gives no build and its related articles are dated December 2024 [18]. The two sources differ on whether a Bandage ends bleeding or subtracts a fixed 50, and the discrepancy is unresolved (see Common Pitfalls).

**Explosions.** The wiki gives crafting data only for the Timed Explosive Charge and Satchel Charge, with no damage figures [16][17]. The Rocket page describes "large splash damage" and gives only rocket counts for structures [15]. The Livestock Update added client prediction when throwing a grenade, C4 or satchel, which affects feel rather than damage [1].

**Falls.** A community FAQ states that fall damage exists and that over 20 damage produces an audible crunch; the page carries no date or build [19]. The Livestock Update lists no fall-damage change [1].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Match armour to the damage type you expect, not to a single protection number

- **Guidance:** Compare protection per damage type and body area before choosing gear, and weigh cold penalties for items such as the Road Sign Jacket.
- **Evidence basis:** Protection is listed per damage type and slot [11][12][13], and some items carry negative values [12].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The item values are primary, but how items stack is unsourced.
- **So what:** A head item with high melee and projectile protection covers only the head [11]; a chest item with low values and a cold penalty can be a poor trade [12].

## Guidance 2 — Treat wiki damage figures as base values, not outcomes

- **Guidance:** Use listed damage and headshot multipliers for relative comparison only.
- **Evidence basis:** Wiki pages list base damage and a multiplier [3][7], protection reduces damage by body area [2][11], and attachments change it [3].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The inputs are primary; the combined result is inference.
- **So what:** Do not expect a listed 50 damage to land as 50 against armoured targets.

## Guidance 3 — Carry more than one bleeding fix until the Bandage behaviour is settled

- **Guidance:** Do not rely on a single Bandage after heavy damage.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki value is -50 [14], and the community article is the only source for the bleed formula [18].
- **Confidence:** Low. The two sources conflict and the formula is single-source.
- **So what:** Check the bleeding value in game after bandaging.

title: Rust Electricity and Logic

text:
This document goes deeper than the game mechanics foundation on Rust's electrical system: the power sources (solar panel, wind turbine, small generator), the rechargeable batteries, the wire tool, and the logic and switching components (switch, timer, counter, memory cell, AND, OR, XOR, RAND, blocker, splitter, branch, combiner). Values come from the Facepunch Rust Wiki item pages, which are first-party, and from Facepunch devblogs that record when behaviour changed.

Confidence is Medium. Item stats are Primary and consistent, but the wiki pages do not state which build they reflect, several mechanics (fuel burn rate, wire limits, power cost of most devices) are not on any page opened, and the wiki shows values that differ from the 2019 devblog (small battery), so some figures may lag the live game.
title: Rust Electricity and Logic

text:
- Three craftable power sources exist on the wiki pages checked: the Large Solar Panel (20 rW) [1], the Wind Turbine (150 rW) [2] and the Small Generator (40 rW, fuelled by Low Grade Fuel) [3].
- The Large, Medium and Small Rechargeable Batteries list 24000, 9000 and 400 rWm capacity and 100, 50 and 15 rW output respectively [4][5][6].
- Solar output depends on sun intensity and the panel's angle to the sun [1]; wind turbine output varies with wind speed [2].
- Since the April 2024 devblog, logic gates no longer need power; active components such as turrets, sensors and lights still do [24].
- The Auto Turret lists 10 rW consumption [21]; the HBHF Sensor lists 1 rW [20].
- The Wire Tool is known by default and costs 2 High Quality Metal [7].
- Several logic parts (timer, counter, memory cell, AND, OR, XOR) craft from Metal Fragments only [8][9][10][11][12][13].
title: Rust Electricity and Logic

text: Covers power generation, storage, wiring and logic components in vanilla Rust (PC) as documented on the Facepunch wiki and devblogs. It does not cover turrets and other deployables in depth (see rust-turrets-deployables), industrial automation, or plugin-based electrical behaviour. Build checked: Livestock Update, 1 October 2026 (the wiki pages themselves do not state a build).
title: Rust Electricity and Logic

text:
- **rW (Rust Watt):** the unit of electrical power production and consumption on item pages [1][4].
- **rWm (Rust Watt Minutes):** battery storage; the number of minutes of discharge at 1 power unit the battery holds [25].
- **Passthrough:** power that a component forwards to its output, for example the Timer passes power for a duration [8].
- **Control input:** a non-power input such as Toggle On, Set, Reset or Switch Off [8][10][15].
title: Rust Electricity and Logic

text:
**Power sources.** The Large Solar Panel produces 20 rW, with output depending on sun intensity and the panel's angle to the sun [1]. The Wind Turbine lists 150 rW and its description says the amount generated varies with wind speed [2]. The Small Generator is powered by Low Grade Fuel and outputs 40 power; it has Force Start and Force Stop control inputs [3]. The page does not give a fuel consumption rate [3].

**Batteries.** Capacity is measured in rWm, the minutes of discharge at 1 power unit [25]. The Large Battery lists 100 rW production and 24000 rWm capacity with a Fully Charged signal output [4]. The Medium Battery lists 50 rW and 9000 rWm; its page says it needs a minimum charge of 5 seconds to discharge, charges at a rate depending on power input with a maximum 80 percent efficiency, and can be wired in series [5]. The Small Battery lists 15 rW and 400 rWm [6]. The 2018 devblog states that batteries must have at least 5 seconds of juice to begin discharging and that batteries were fixed to wire in series [26].

**Wiring.** The Wire Tool connects electrical objects: aim at an object, click an input or output handle, then click another object's handle; holding right mouse clears or cancels a connection [7]. The page does not state connection limits [7].

**Switching and logic.** Each component below is described by its wiki page.

- **Switch:** inputs Power In, Switch On, Switch Off; output Power Out [15].
- **Button:** a simple electric button with Power In and Power Out [22].
- **Timer:** passes power through for a duration; inputs Power In and Toggle On [8].
- **Counter:** inputs Power In, Increment, Decrement, Clear; output Passthrough, which allows passthrough when a target is reached [9].
- **Memory Cell:** a 1-bit storage component; Set stores 1, Reset stores 0, Toggle flips the state, and it has an Output and an Inverted Output [10].
- **AND Switch:** passes power only when both inputs receive power, with the passthrough amount the greater of the two sources [11].
- **OR Switch:** passthrough amount is the greater of either power source [12].
- **XOR Switch:** passes power only if exactly one input receives power [13].
- **RAND Switch:** each time the Set input receives power it rolls true or false to allow passthrough [17].
- **Blocker:** prevents passthrough while power is received on its Block Passthrough input [14].
- **Splitter:** splits a signal into 3; the output amount is the input divided by the number of output slots in use [16].
- **Electrical Branch:** branches power off a main line by a set amount, with Branch Out and Power Out [18].
- **Root Combiner:** combines two root electrical sources into one signal; it can be wired in series but cannot be used with components that do not produce energy [19].
- **Sensors:** the Pressure Pad allows power to flow while a player stands on it [23]; the HBHF Sensor's passthrough equals the number of humans detected in a 10 m radius [20].

text:
- Treating old guides as current: the logic gates stopped needing power in April 2024 [24], so older wiring advice about gate power cost is outdated.
- Placing solar panels outside building privilege: they decay there [28].
- Expecting a combiner to merge anything: it works only with energy-producing sources [19].
- Expecting a battery to discharge immediately: it needs a minimum charge to begin [5][26].
- Expecting AND or OR to sum their inputs: both pass the greater of the two sources [11][12].

text: Electricity powers the Auto Turret [21]; see rust-turrets-deployables for turret behaviour and rust-raiding-costs-defence for defence costs. The wiki lists further electrical consumers such as the Electric Furnace, Electric Heater, Water Pump, Elevator and Industrial Conveyor [29]; their consumption values were not opened here. Workbench tiers gate crafting (see rust-items-crafting-foundation) and the parent system overview is in rust-game-mechanics-foundation.
title: Rust Electricity and Logic

text:
## Guidance 1 — Pair solar or wind with a battery rather than wiring them straight to loads

- **Guidance:** Treat solar and wind as variable sources and put a battery between them and critical loads.
- **Evidence basis:** Solar output varies with sun and angle [1]; wind turbine output varies with wind speed [2]; batteries store energy in rWm [4][25].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The variability is cited, but the design recommendation is inference.
- **So what:** A base running turrets is less likely to lose power when output dips.

## Guidance 2 — Do not budget power for logic gates, but do for sensors and turrets

- **Guidance:** When estimating load, count active devices and ignore logic gates.
- **Evidence basis:** Gates lost power requirements in April 2024 [24]; turret and sensor consumption is listed [21][20].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The devblog is Primary but the wiki pages list no gate consumption, so the absence is inferred.
- **So what:** Smaller generators suffice for gate-heavy circuits.

## Guidance 3 — Verify numbers in game before building a large circuit

- **Guidance:** Check item inspect values in game after each monthly update.
- **Evidence basis:** Small Battery values differ between wiki and 2019 devblog [6][25]; wiki pages state no build.
- **Confidence:** High. The discrepancy itself is documented.
- **So what:** Avoid relying on remembered figures.

title: Rust Fishing

text:
This document covers Rust fishing: the Handmade Fishing Rod, bait, the casting and reeling minigame, the fish that exist, what a catch is used for, the April 2026 overfishing rule, and the role of fishing villages as buyers of catches. It goes deeper than the mechanics foundation and does not restate it.

Rod, bait and minigame controls are well sourced from the Facepunch devblog that introduced fishing in August 2021 [1] and the Facepunch wiki [3][4]. Numeric values (bait values, catch odds, scrap prices, gutting yields, overfishing timers) are not published on any page opened, so they are absent rather than guessed. The document is rated Medium: primary sources agree on the mechanics, but the numbers a player would want are missing and the 2021 devblog predates later rebalances.
title: Rust Fishing

text:
- Fishing was introduced in the 5 August 2021 Going Deep update; the devblog describes the Handmade Fishing Rod as "fully functional and ready for use" [1].
- The Handmade Fishing Rod costs 200 Wood and 2 Rope, needs no workbench, takes 10 s to craft without one, and "requires bait" [4].
- Bait goes in the rod's lure slot; foods can be bait, and worms and grubs can drop when harvesting berries, hemp and potatoes, with double the chance on player-planted crops [1].
- Catch requirements depend on bait value, water type, water depth and location [1].
- Spring Clean (2 April 2026) added overfishing: a heavily fished area returns only junk until it repopulates, and fish traps are not affected [2].
- Since Spring Clean, Herring and Anchovy can no longer be caught in the deep sea [2].
- Catches can be eaten, gutted for resources, or sold for scrap at a fishing village [1][3].
- The Livestock update (1 Oct 2026) contains no fishing change on the page opened [11].
title: Rust Fishing

text: Covers vanilla PC Rust fishing as documented up to the Livestock update (1 Oct 2026). Plugin-driven fishing changes and Underwater Labs fishing detail beyond one wiki mention are excluded. Boat and submarine mechanics belong to rust-vehicles. Cooking and hunger values belong to rust-farming-food.
title: Rust Fishing

text:
- **Lure slot:** the rod slot in which bait is equipped [1].
- **Bait value:** a per-food number shown in item info that affects what can be caught [1]. Individual values were not found.
- **Overfished:** an area in which too many fish were caught within a time window, so casts return only junk [2].
- **Fish trap:** a passive fishing deployable that overfishing does not affect [2].
title: Rust Fishing

text:
**Evidence layer.**

**Rod.** The wiki names the Handmade Fishing Rod as the fishing rod. It can be obtained from missions, fishing villages, large fishing villages or crafting [3]. Use attack2 to cast and wait for a bite [4].

**Bait.** The devblog says a bait must be equipped in the rod's lure slot, foods can serve as bait, and each food's bait value is in its item info [1]. The wiki says bait comes from foraging, hunting animals and food crates [3]. Worms and grubs can drop while harvesting resources such as berries, hemp and potatoes, and plants the player planted give double the chance [1]. The Worm item is described as usable as bait [10].

**Casting and reeling.** Hold right mouse while aiming at water, then left-click to cast [1][3]. After a wait a fish bites and a minigame starts [3]. A and D pull the fish left or right and S reels it in; pulling it side to side tires it so it moves less [1]. Reeling and pulling strain the line, and if strained too much the line snaps and the fish escapes; the rod shakes and plays audio cues under strain [1]. Players are told to pause reeling when tension is high and keep the fish centred [3].

**Where fish come from.** The wiki lists fishing areas as Swamp, River, Ocean and the Underwater Lab moon pool [3]. The devblog says catches depend on bait value, water type, depth and location [1].

**Fish.** The devblog lists eight fish: Herring, Anchovy, Sardines, Yellow Perch, Catfish, Small Sharks, Salmon and Orange Roughy [1]. The wiki sidebar additionally lists Minnows and Small Trout [3].

**Uses.** A catch can be eaten, sold for scrap, or gutted for loot, and selling requires a fishing village [3]. The devblog says gutting yields resources and that catches can be taken to any fishing village for scrap [1]. Salmon, Catfish and Orange Roughy descriptions say their stomachs can hold random items [6][7][9].

**Overfishing.** Fish caught in an area within a set time window can make it overfished; casts there return only junk until the area repopulates after a refresh period [2]. Facepunch states that many ConVars let servers adjust or disable the feature, that it targets AFK fish farming in bases, and that fish traps are unaffected [2].

**Fishing villages.** The 2021 devblog says villages sell boats, submarines and torpedoes and that village spawning was improved [1]. Fishing villages are also a source of the rod [3].

title: Rust Fishing

text:
## Guidance 1 — Fish away from your base and rotate spots

- **Guidance:** Fish at natural waters and move on once casts start returning junk, rather than farming one spot.
- **Evidence basis:** Overfishing makes heavily fished areas return only junk until they repopulate [2]; fishing in bases is called out as unintended [2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The mechanic is primary-sourced, but window and refresh durations are unpublished.
- **So what:** Expect diminishing returns at one spot; do not build a fishing setup around AFK casting.

## Guidance 2 — Stock worms by harvesting your own crops

- **Guidance:** Keep a stack of worms by harvesting planted berries, hemp or potatoes.
- **Evidence basis:** Worms and grubs drop from harvesting, with double chance on planted crops [1]; worms are bait [10].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Drop rates and bait values are not published.
- **So what:** A small planter doubles as a bait source, though whether worms are the best bait is unverified.

## Guidance 3 — Treat fish-for-scrap as an unverified income route

- **Guidance:** Do not plan a scrap economy around fish until prices are checked in game.
- **Evidence basis:** Villages buy catches for scrap [1][3], but no rate was found in any opened source.
- **Confidence:** Low. The existence of the trade is sourced; the value is not.
- **So what:** Test one sale at a village before committing time.

title: Rust Game Mechanics: Foundation

text:
This document is an overview of the core survival loop in Rust (Facepunch Studios, PC): the vital statistics a character must manage (health, hunger, thirst), the environmental pressures (radiation, cold and heat), the helpers (comfort, healing items), the failure states (bleeding, wounded, death), respawn through sleeping bags, the effect of server wipes on progression, and a first look at monuments. Deeper treatment belongs in later deep-dive documents.

The most recent Facepunch update at the time of checking is the Livestock Update of 1 October 2026 [1][2], whose notes list no change to health, hunger, thirst, temperature or respawn mechanics [2]. Item-level numbers come from the Facepunch wiki [3][4][5][6][7][8][9]. Threshold values for hunger, thirst and wounded recovery come only from a community guide [13], so the document-level confidence is Medium: several thresholds have no primary source, and sources conflict on one value.
title: Rust Game Mechanics: Foundation

text:
- The latest Facepunch news post at the time of checking is the Livestock Update, dated Thursday 1 October 2026 [1][2].
- That update lists no changes to health, hunger, thirst, temperature or respawn mechanics [2].
- Water gives Hydration +30 over 5 seconds and Radiation -5 over 4 seconds on the wiki (checked against the 1 October 2026 build) [5].
- A Large Medkit removes 100 bleeding and, if carried in the toolbar, guarantees recovery from the wounded state [7].
- A Sleeping Bag sets a respawn point for you or an assigned player, with a long cooldown that the wiki does not quantify [4].
- Forced wipes land on the first Thursday of the month with Facepunch's monthly update, and blueprints are not automatically reset [14].
- Monuments are grouped by a community guide into tiers by keycard and radiation, and the Outpost and Bandit Camp are safe zones [15].

text:
- **Wounded:** a state entered when a non-lethal hit takes health to zero; the player crawls and may recover or be revived [13].
- **Comfort:** a beneficial effect from being near comfort items [13].
- **Forced wipe:** the monthly wipe that accompanies Facepunch's update [14].
- **Monument:** a pre-generated map landmark with loot and NPCs [15].
title: Rust Game Mechanics: Foundation

text:
**Evidence layer.** Figures marked community-sourced come from a single guide dated 11 June 2026 that states no game build [13].

**Vital stats.** The Facepunch wiki lists consumables as changing hydration, calories and healing over time; for example Water gives Hydration +30 and Healing over time +5, each over 5 seconds [5], and a Can of Beans gives Calories +100, Healing over time +4 and Hydration +25 [8]. A community guide states that a character is dehydrated when hydration falls below about 25, causing slow health and movement-speed loss, and that empty hunger causes steady health loss [13].

**Radiation.** Radiation is picked up in certain areas such as monuments, and higher-tier radiation can still pass through a Hazmat Suit, which gives 50% radiation protection according to a community guide [13]. Anti-Radiation Pills lower radiation and can dehydrate you [6]. Water slightly lowers radiation [5]. A Geiger Counter is a tool item [9]. The Livestock Update fixed Oil Rig radiation starting before the locked crate is looted [2].

**Temperature.** The community guide gives only qualitative cues: nights are colder, snow biomes are harsh, and a wet character gets colder [13]. It gives no numeric temperature thresholds [13]. A Camp Fire "provides warmth and light, and you can cook with it" [10].

**Comfort and regeneration.** Per the community guide, a Campfire roughly doubles the health regeneration tick, a Campfire or running Furnace raises comfort to about 50%, and a chair or Bear Skin Rug can raise it to 100%. Comfort heals only while hunger and hydration are above their low thresholds [13].

**Bleeding, wounded, death.** The Bandage has Instant Health +5 and Bleeding -50 [11]. The Large Medkit removes 100 bleeding, gives +100 healing over time, and guarantees recovery from the wounded state when in the toolbar [7]. Per the guide, wounded recovery takes about 45 seconds before a roll, with a base chance of about 20% and about 45% with maxed food and hydration, and teammates can revive with a Large Medkit or Medical Syringe [13]. Fall damage never causes wounded [13].

**Respawn.** A Sleeping Bag is "a place to respawn, with a long cooldown", is craftable for 30 Cloth, and despawns as a dropped item after 20 minutes [4].

**Wipes and progression.** A forced wipe removes bases, loot and resources and generates a new procedural map; it does not automatically reset blueprints, and blueprint wipes are a server-by-server choice [14]. Facepunch's own wiki documents the scheduled wipe: default Thursday 19:00 London time, with monthly, biweekly or weekly tags [12].

**PvP/PvE loop and monuments (overview).** A community guide describes tiered monuments from Supermarket and Gas Station to Launch Site and Military Tunnels, a three-tier keycard ladder, and hostile NPC scientists and players competing for loot, with Outpost and Bandit Camp as safe zones [15].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Treat community threshold numbers as provisional and verify in game

- **Guidance:** Use the community thresholds (hydration about 25, wounded odds) as rough planning values only.
- **Evidence basis:** The thresholds come from a single guide with no stated build [13], and the pill hydration value conflicts with the Facepunch wiki [6].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Documented item values are primary, but thresholds are single-source.
- **So what:** Check the in-game HUD and the current wiki before building a strategy on exact figures.

## Guidance 2 — Carry healing for both bleeding and the wounded state

- **Guidance:** Keep a Bandage for routine bleeding and a Large Medkit for the highest-risk fights.
- **Evidence basis:** The Bandage removes 50 bleeding [11]; the Large Medkit removes 100 bleeding and guarantees wounded recovery from the toolbar [7].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Item effects are wiki facts, while the tactical recommendation is judgement.
- **So what:** Fewer deaths in sustained fights, at the price of scarce Medkit materials.

## Guidance 3 — Plan progression around the wipe, and check the server's blueprint policy

- **Guidance:** Expect base and map loss monthly, and read each server's blueprint wipe rule before investing in research.
- **Evidence basis:** Forced wipes follow the monthly update and blueprints are not automatically reset [14][12].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The blueprint policy is described by a commercial guide, not by Facepunch.
- **So what:** Time big projects early in a wipe cycle.

text:
This deep-dive goes beyond the monument overview in rust-game-mechanics-foundation. It covers how the Facepunch wiki groups monuments (safe zone, small, large), what the three keycards and the Electric Fuse are, how the 2026 power-grid work (Heavy Fuses, the Power Plant, Monument Blockers, Powergrid loot rooms) changed monument progression, and what individual monuments are known for.

The official Facepunch material is strong on the 2026 changes and on item data, but it does not publish a per-monument tier table or monument loot tables. The tier-by-card ladder comes only from a community guide that gives no build number, and the only official tier list is from 2018. Overall confidence is Medium: item and devblog facts are primary, monument tiering is community-derived.
title: Rust Monuments and Loot

text:
- The Facepunch wiki sorts monuments into safe zone, small and large groups; the safe-zone group is Bandit Camp, Outpost, Fishing Village, Large Fishing Village, Large Barn and Ranch [1].
- Green, Blue and Red Keycards cannot be crafted, repaired, recycled or researched; they despawn after 20 minutes, 40 minutes and 1 hour respectively [2][3][4].
- Green Keycards drop from scientists at a stated 36.3% chance (1-2 cards) for most scientist variants, per the wiki loot table [2].
- The Electric Fuse is recyclable, stacks to 10 and despawns after 40 minutes; the wiki lists its loot sources by percentage [5].
- From August 2026 the Power Plant takes Heavy Fuses to power an island grid; the Livestock Update added Powergrid loot rooms at monuments that unlock with enough Heavy Fuses [6][7].
- Monument Blockers (September 2026) slow early access at monuments with red keycard puzzle rooms; unbroken blockers start to decay after 24 hours [8].
- A per-monument tier table (card, radiation, loot) exists only in a community guide with no build number *(assessed as community-derived)* [13].
title: Rust Monuments and Loot

text: Covered: monument categories, safe zones, keycards, fuses and Heavy Fuses, the 2026 power-grid system, puzzle mechanics from the official 2018 devblog (flagged as historical), and what monuments are known for, on vanilla PC servers, checked against the Livestock Update of 1 October 2026. Not covered: per-monument loot tables (no primary source publishes them, see Open Questions), raiding mechanics (rust-raiding-costs-defence), vehicles (rust-vehicles), farming and food (rust-farming-food), map generation (rust-wipes-map-generation), modded servers and consoles.
title: Rust Monuments and Loot

text:
- **Monument:** a larger, build-protected area with buildings and entities that players visit for loot, recycling, trading or combat [1].
- **Safe zone:** a monument where hostile actions make you a target for NPCs and turrets [1].
- **Keycard:** Green, Blue or Red access item used at locked puzzle rooms [2][3][4].
- **Heavy Fuse:** a fuse loaded into special fuse boxes at the Power Plant to power the island grid [6].
- **Powergrid loot room:** a locked room at a monument that opens once enough Heavy Fuses power the grid [7].
- **Monument Blocker:** an obstacle added to monuments with red keycard puzzle rooms [8].
title: Rust Monuments and Loot

text:
**Monument groups.** The wiki's Map page says monuments are larger build-protected areas that players visit for loot, recycling, trading or combat, and splits them into three groups [1]. Safe zone: Bandit Camp, Outpost, Fishing Village, Large Fishing Village, Large Barn, Ranch. Small: Abandoned Supermarket, Abandoned Cabins, Lighthouse, Mining Outpost, Oxums Gas Station, Quarry. Large: Airfield, Abandoned Military Base, Arctic Research Base, Giant Excavator Pit, Harbor, Junkyard, Launch Site, Large Oil Rig, Oil Rig, Underwater Lab, Military Tunnels, Power Plant, Satellite Dish, Sewer Branch, The Dome, Train Yard, Water Treatment Plant [1]. The same page says the Harbor is where the Cargo Ship stops to drop locked crates, and that the three ocean monuments are good component sources [1]. The page describes only a few monuments in detail [1].

**Safe zones.** The wiki states that in safe-zone monuments you can trade with NPCs, hostile actions make you a target for NPCs and turrets, and players can only be hurt by other players outside the zones [1]. The Outpost has a safe zone spanning the whole monument, sentry turrets inside and around it, two entrances plus underground tunnels, vending machines, a drone shop, and stations including a Workbench Level 1, Research Table, Oil Refinery, Recycler, Barbecue and Repair Bench [10]. The Power Trip devblog stopped ore nodes and woodpiles spawning in safe zones and left the yellow (safe zone) recyclers unchanged [6]. A community guide adds that turrets enforce the rule, so drawing a weapon is unwise [13].

**Keycards.** Each of the three cards stacks to 1 and cannot be crafted, repaired, recycled or researched [2][3][4]. The wiki describes Green as low-level clearance for basic areas and Blue as medium-level clearance [2][3]; Red is described as high clearance for top-level areas [4]. Wiki Green Keycard loot data lists scientists (1-2 cards, 36.3%), Road Scientist (1 card, 23.6%), and Peacekeeper Scientist and Bandit Guard (1 card, 16.7%) [2]. The Blue and Red pages give no loot sources [3][4]. The community guide describes a ladder in which each card opens rooms whose reward includes the next card [13].

**Fuses.** The Electric Fuse is described as unreliable and allows electrical passthrough for a limited time [5]. It drops from Tech Parts 1 (1-2 items, 26.5%), several crate types (14.3% each) and various scientists (4.7% each), among other sources [5]. It recycles into 24 scrap in a Recycler and 16 scrap in a Safe Zone Recycler, both stated at 100% chance [5]. The Safe Zone Recycler returns 40% of recyclable material value at 8 seconds per item [11]. The community guide says many puzzles need power: find a fuse, insert it and flip switches in the right order [13].

**Power Plant and Heavy Fuses (Power Trip, August 2026).** Heavy Fuses are found as loot and inserted into special fuse boxes at the Power Plant; running it powers the island-wide grid [6]. Power affects recyclers: green recyclers outside safe zones run at 50% efficiency rising to 60% with sufficient power, and cycle time drops from 5 to 4.5 seconds at maximum power; a new red recycler at the Power Plant gives 75% and works only at maximum power [6]. The devblog also added another loot room reachable only with sufficient power [6].

**Player-maintained monuments (August 2026).** Per the same devblog: the Abandoned Supermarket freezer gives steady chilled food while powered; Water Treatment Plant pipes stay empty until the plant is maintained; Oxum's Gas Station garage door and car lift work when powered; Airfield Control Tower terminals raise air drop frequency or enable a Chinook crate drop and drain over time [6]. At Launch Site a Satellite Control Computer lets players crash a satellite, which spills loot crates [6]. On the two oil rigs, a switch (available once the Power Plant runs) pumps crude to the Dome for 20 minutes on the Large rig and at half that rate on the Small rig; both on gives 1.5x crude [6].

**Monument Blockers and the marketplace (September 2026).** Blockers appear on monuments with red keycard puzzle rooms; heavy ones need significant damage and do not respawn, a handful can be destroyed by melee, and any not destroyed within 24 hours start to decay [8]. The drone marketplace needs the Power Plant: its battery rises slowly with 4 or more active fuses, accepts purchases at 50%, and does not drain while at least one fuse is inserted [8].

**Powergrid loot rooms (October 2026).** The Livestock devblog lists monuments with new rooms: Airfield, Ferry Terminal, Harbour 1, Harbour 2, Junkyard, Launch Site, Military Tunnels, Nuclear Missile Silo, Radtown, Sewer Branch, Trainyard and Water Treatment Plant [7]. The post lists Ferry Terminal twice, so the unique count is 12 although 13 entries appear [7]. Rooms are locked until enough Heavy Fuses power the grid; harder monuments need more; no per-monument fuse counts are given [7].

**Heavy Fuse decay.** Power Plant heavy fuse decay scales with server population: 4x longer at 10 or fewer players, normal at 100 or more; the convars are `powergrid.fusedecaylowpop`, `fusedecayhighpop` and `fusedecaylowpopscale` [7]. The post also moved the small heavy fuse box at the Power Plant so it is reachable from outside through a broken window [7].

**Puzzle design (2018, historical).** The Puzzle Update introduced Entity I/O circuits (generator, switch, timed switch, splitter, AND, OR, card reader, wheel switch, push button) and linked monuments into a path of rising difficulty [12]. It stated cards were found in puzzles, usually the final loot room, with 10 uses each, and electric fuses lasted 180 seconds [12]. These 2018 values are not confirmed for the current build.

text:
## Guidance 1 — Check the current update before relying on any tier list

- **Guidance:** Treat any monument tier list, including this document's community table, as provisional and confirm in game or in the latest devblog.
- **Evidence basis:** The only official tiers are from 2018 [12], the current tier table has no build [13], and three consecutive updates changed monument systems [6][7][8].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The change history is primary, but the advice is a judgement.
- **So what:** Do not plan a run around a card requirement you have not seen this wipe.

## Guidance 2 — Scientists are a documented Green Keycard source, so low-tier cards need not wait on puzzles

- **Guidance:** If you need a Green Keycard, fighting scientists is a documented route as well as puzzle rooms.
- **Evidence basis:** Wiki drop rates of 36.3% for most scientist variants [2]; the guide agrees green cards appear at starter monuments [13].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Rates are primary but depend on the live loot table, and the wiki has no Blue or Red source data.
- **So what:** Expect fights, not just puzzles, on the way to the first card.

## Guidance 3 — On low-population servers, expect Heavy Fuses to last longer

- **Guidance:** Admins running small servers can lean on the population scaling and adjust the three convars if power phases feel wrong.
- **Evidence basis:** The Livestock devblog states 4x longer decay at 10 or fewer players and names the convars, with no defaults listed [7].
- **Confidence:** High. This is a direct Facepunch statement, though values may be retuned.
- **So what:** Read the default values from your own server before changing anything.

## Guidance 4 — Destroy or bypass Monument Blockers early in the wipe only if you can afford the noise

- **Guidance:** Blockers decay after 24 hours, so a patient group can wait rather than spend explosives.
- **Evidence basis:** Heavy blockers need significant damage and do not respawn, and undestroyed blockers decay after 24 hours [8].
- **Confidence:** Low. The trade-off is inference; Facepunch gives no HP or cost figures [8].
- **So what:** Compare the cost of damaging a blocker with the cost of waiting, once you have measured the HP yourself.

title: Rust Teams and Clans

text:
Rust has two social grouping systems: the long-standing team, and the clan system added by the Common Ground update on 2 July 2026. Facepunch documents how teams are created and what they share, and its softcore post gives the only Facepunch-stated team cap (4, which also bounds Tool Cupboard and Autoturret authorisation in that mode). Facepunch's Common Ground post describes clans, the Clan Table, a clan chat channel and the hardcore exclusion [1][2][3].

Most numbers that players ask about are not in a Facepunch source I could open. The default vanilla team size, the clan member cap, clan permissions and cross-server behaviour come only from community write-ups. Document confidence is therefore Low.
title: Rust Teams and Clans

text:
- Teams are created from a button at the bottom left of the inventory screen, invited by pressing E near a player, and accepted via "join team". Members see each other on the map, share markers and have team chat [2].
- Softcore servers cap teams at 4, and Facepunch states this includes the number of people who can authorise at a Tool Cupboard or on an Autoturret (softcore launch post, 4 Feb 2021) [1].
- Clans are described by Facepunch as "a more advanced version of teams where you can have more members with different roles/permissions", with a separate chat channel and announcement text, managed at Clan Tables [3].
- The clan system is disabled in hardcore mode [3].
- Tool Cupboard authorisation is per player: the placer is authorised automatically and others press E at the cupboard [4].
- Two community guides give a default team size of 8; one names the convar `relationshipmanager.maxteamsize` (0 disables teams). Facepunch's Server Gamemodes wiki also names that convar for changing the maximum team and auth size under Softcore settings [10]; the Teams and Useful Commands wiki pages state neither the convar nor a default team size [9][6][2].
- A community guide gives a clan cap of 100 and a convar `clan.maxmembercount` defaulting to 100; this is not Facepunch-confirmed [7].

text:
- **Team:** the in-game party of players created from the inventory screen [2].
- **Clan:** the Common Ground clan system, managed at a Clan Table [3].
- **Clan Table:** the deployable at which clans are created and managed [3].
- **Group limit:** a server rule capping how many players may play together; an admin policy, not a Facepunch-documented game rule [6].
title: Rust Teams and Clans

text:
**Teams.** Create a team with the button at the bottom left of the inventory. Invite by standing near a player until the "invite to team" prompt shows and pressing E. The invitee accepts with "join team". Members see each other on the map, share markers and chat in team chat. Team chat shares a location with global text chat and Tab switches between them. The wiki page states no size limit and does not mention voice [2].

**Softcore team cap.** Softcore launched on 4 Feb 2021 with a maximum team size of 4, which Facepunch says includes the number of people who can authorise at a Tool Cupboard or on an Autoturret [1]. The Common Ground post does not restate this value [3].

**Authorisation.** Whoever places a Tool Cupboard is authorised automatically, and others walk up and press E. An authorised player can deauthorise themselves by holding E, and anyone with access can clear the whole list. Authorisation grants building and pickup within the radius and access to privilege-gated traps [4]. A community guide adds that turrets keep their own authorisation list, that teammates are not authorised automatically, and that code locks are shared by entering the placer's code once, with a separate guest code [6]. The Facepunch Code Lock page opened here says only that it is an electronic lock with a four-digit code [5].

**Clans.** Per the Common Ground post, clans allow more members than teams, with roles and permissions, a separate clan chat channel and announcement text. They are created and managed at Clan Tables, clan names appear on nameplates, and nearby members' locations show on the map [3]. Community guide detail written before launch (June 2026): ranks are customisable with permissions including Set MOTD, Edit Banner, Access Logs, Invite, Kick, Promote and Demote; rank changes and invites need the player to be in range of a Clan Table; Clan Tables are at the Outpost and Bandit Camp and are craftable after researching at a Level 1 Workbench; clans are said to span servers and survive map wipes [7].

**Voice and chat.** The Facepunch wiki chat page could not be opened (404). The Common Ground changelog mentions voice-chat delay and computer-station voice fixes, and a fix for inviting players to a party in the in-game friends list [3]. No Facepunch source opened documents proximity or team voice rules.
