title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
A Rust Oxide plugin is a single C# source file (`.cs`) that the framework compiles at runtime. It holds one public class in the `Oxide.Plugins` namespace, inheriting from `RustPlugin` (or `CovalencePlugin` for game-agnostic plugins), decorated with an `[Info]` attribute for name, author and version [1][2]. Behaviour is added by writing hook methods the framework calls on game events, by registering commands, and by registering permissions [1][2][4][5]. Settings live in a JSON config file in `oxide/config`, persistent state in JSON data files in `oxide/data`, and translated messages in `oxide/lang/<code>/<Plugin>.json` [7][16][17][18].

Carbon, the alternative loader, documents the same plugin shape: `RustPlugin` in `Oxide.Plugins` for Oxide-compatible plugins, and `CarbonPlugin` in `Carbon.Plugins` for Carbon-only plugins [19]. Where Carbon differs (hook dispatch, extra command attributes, config folder name) this document labels the difference only where a Carbon page states it [20][21][23]. Confidence is Medium: structure and API are primary-sourced from the framework docs, but several pages are thin (no signatures on the core permission library page, no description on some hook pages), and the Oxide docs say nothing on how conflicting hook return values from several plugins are resolved.
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
- Oxide plugins are distributed as `.cs` files; extensions are `.dll` files [1][2].
- The main class is public, lives in `Oxide.Plugins` and inherits `RustPlugin` for Rust-only plugins [2]. The plugin guidelines say the file name should match the main class name in PascalCase [8].
- Metadata is `[Info("Name", "Author", "1.0.0")]` plus an optional `[Description("...")]` [2][4][8].
- Lifecycle order is Init, Loaded, OnServerInitialized, then (on shutdown) Shutdown and Unload [3].
- For hooks documented with return behaviour, a non-null return overrides default behaviour and null lets it proceed (`CanLootEntity`); many hooks list "No return behavior" [12][13][14][15].
- Oxide's hook index grouped hooks into 38 categories on 2026-10-08, the largest being Player (155), Entity (102), Item (64) and Vehicle (52) [11].
- Permissions are registered with `permission.RegisterPermission(name, this)`, and the documented convention is `pluginname.permission` in lowercase [5][8].
- Carbon says its folder and plugin structure matches Oxide, but Oxide's `config` folder becomes `configs` and commands use a `c.` prefix instead of `o.` [23][28].
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
Covered: structure and APIs of server-side C# plugins for Rust on Oxide (uMod) and Carbon: class and attributes, lifecycle, hooks and their return semantics, commands, permissions API, config, data files and localization files, development environment, and official authoring guidelines. Build: Oxide.Rust 2.0.7810 and Carbon v2.0.262 era (Rust 2634.289.1, October 2026).

Not covered: installing frameworks and the admin-side permission commands (see rust-modding-plugins-foundation), individual plugin reviews, the Rust game systems hooks touch (see rust-combat-damage-model, rust-weapons-ammo, rust-raiding-costs-defence), console and client modification, and Carbon module/UI libraries beyond a mention.
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
- **Hook:** a function called by the game or by Oxide to define what happens on a game event [1].
- **Info attribute:** the metadata attribute carrying plugin name, author and version [2][4].
- **Covalence plugin:** a game-agnostic plugin deriving from `CovalencePlugin`, versus a `RustPlugin` for Rust only [2].
- **Data file:** JSON persistence in `oxide/data`, distinct from the admin-edited config in `oxide/config` [7][17].
- **Harmony patch:** a runtime method patch installed with `[AutoPatch]` plus `[HarmonyPatch]`, available in both frameworks' docs [4][20].
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
**Plugin file and class.** A plugin is one `.cs` file compiled at runtime; the beginner guide names both file and class `MyFirstPlugin`, uses the `Oxide.Plugins` namespace, and derives from `RustPlugin` [2]. The guidelines state the file name "should match the name of your main class and use PascalCase" [8]. Carbon's first-plugin page uses the file-scoped namespace form (`namespace Oxide.Plugins;`) for Oxide-compatible plugins [19]. Compile errors appear in the server console after the file is uploaded [2].

**Development environment.** Oxide's guide names Visual Studio, Visual Studio Code and JetBrains Rider as IDE options, and lists `Oxide.Core.dll`, `Oxide.Rust.dll`, `Assembly-CSharp.dll` and `UnityEngine.dll` as the references to add [10]. Its best-practices page recommends Git source control (excluding binaries, logs and local config), testing, and documenting installation, commands and configuration [9]. For Carbon, the developer docs describe a local Windows development server built from the Carbon.QuickStart files, with an optional debugger set in `doorstop_config.ini` [25].

**Attributes.** `[Info("Name", "Author", "1.0.0")]`: the name uses spaces between words, the second argument is the developer or maintainer, and the version is three-part [4]. `[Description]` is a brief summary [4]; the guidelines recommend it for documentation [8]. Further documented attributes: `[ChatCommand]`, `[ConsoleCommand]`, `[Command]` (covalence), `[Permission]`, `[PluginReference]`, `[OnlinePlayers]`, `[HookMethod("HookName")]` and `[AutoPatch]`; comment directives `//Requires: PluginName` (plugin will not start if the required plugin is missing) and `//Reference: AssemblyName` [4].

**Lifecycle.** Per Oxide's lifecycle page: `Init` runs first, before dependencies are available, and an exception there stops initialisation; `Loaded` runs after Init and before registration, and is where asynchronously loaded config and localisation can be read through the `Config` object; `OnServerInitialized` runs near the end of boot, and still runs locally on a runtime reload; `Shutdown` runs only if the game provider supports Advanced Hooks; `Unload` runs when the plugin manager unloads the plugin. `OnConfigChanged` can override default config monitoring during hotloading [3]. The beginner guide registers permissions in `Init` [2][5]; the hook page shows `OnServerInitialized(bool serverInitialized)` is called with `true` after startup and with `false` on hot-loaded plugins when the server is already initialised [13].

**Hooks.** Hooks are methods whose name and parameters match a documented hook; the framework calls them when the event fires [1][2]. Each hook has its own page at `/hooks/<category>/<HookName>` giving signature, description where present, return behaviour and the engine call site [11][12]. For `CanLootEntity(BasePlayer player, WorldItem instance)`, the page states that returning a non-null value overrides default behaviour and returning null lets it proceed [12]. Other documented hooks list "No return behavior" (`OnServerInitialized`, `OnUserPermissionGranted`, `OnPlayerConnected`) [13][14][15]. `OnUserPermissionGranted` fires only when the permission is newly added to the user's data [14]. Hook names often come in pairs (for example `OnOvenStart`/`OnOvenStarted`), which is an inference from names, not stated by the index [11].

**Commands.** Rust plugins use `[ChatCommand("name")]` with `(BasePlayer player, string command, string[] args)` and `[ConsoleCommand("name")]` with `(ConsoleSystem.Arg arg)`; covalence plugins use `[Command]` with an `IPlayer` [4]. `[Permission("perm.name")]` restricts a command to holders of that permission [4]. The guidelines ask for lowercase underscore command names such as `my_command` [8].

**Permissions API (Oxide).** Register in `Init` with `permission.RegisterPermission("epicstuff.use", this)`; check with `permission.UserHasPermission("playerID", "epicstuff.use")` or `player.HasPermission(...)` on an `IPlayer`; group management includes `CreateGroup(name, title, rank)`, `GrantGroupPermission`, `RevokeGroupPermission`, `GetGroupPermissions(group, includeParents)`, `AddUserGroup` and `UserHasGroup` [5]. The beginner guide passes `player.UserIDString` to `UserHasPermission` [2]. The core library page confirms `RegisterPermission` makes a permission available for assignment to players and groups, and that `CreateGroup` attaches group title and rank [6].

**Config, data and lang files.** Config lives in `oxide/config/<PluginName>.json` and is the admin-edited layer; data lives in `oxide/data` and is plugin-managed; language files are `oxide/lang/<code>/<Plugin>.json` [7][16][17][18]. A data file is opened with `Interface.Oxide.DataFileSystem.GetFile(Name)`, returning a `DynamicConfigFile` with `ReadObject<T>()`, `WriteObject(obj)` and `Clear()` [7]. Classes are serialised with Newtonsoft.Json; `[JsonProperty(PropertyName=...)]` sets a readable key, `[JsonIgnore]` excludes runtime fields, and `ObjectCreationHandling.Replace` on lists prevents default entries accumulating on every restart [7]. The beginner guide implements config through `LoadConfig`, `LoadDefaultConfig`, `GetDefaultConfig` and `SaveConfig` [2]. The Oxide docs do not describe how plugin code registers messages; admin-facing notes only describe the file layout, `{0}`/`{1}` placeholders and Rust text tags [18].

**Carbon plugin shape.** Carbon documents the same layout for Oxide-compatible plugins and a Carbon-only variant: namespace `Carbon.Plugins`, base class `CarbonPlugin` [19]. Carbon's hook system differs internally: it calls hooks by numeric ID through `HookCaller.CallStaticHook` rather than `Interface.CallHook` with a name string [20]. Its owner-facing comparison says Carbon only runs hooks that loaded plugins need, while Oxide "fires all hooks all the time" (Carbon's wording) [23]. Carbon's hooks reference marks hooks not flagged Static or Patch as applied dynamically when a plugin subscribes [24]. Carbon adds command restriction attributes `[Group]`, `[AuthLevel(n)]` and `[Cooldown(ms)]` beside `[Permission]`, plus `[ProtectedCommand]` [21].

text:
Plugin skeleton elements (docs read 2026-10-08):

| Element | Oxide-compatible form | Source |
|---------|-----------------------|--------|
| Namespace | `Oxide.Plugins` | [2][19] |
| Base class | `RustPlugin` (Rust) or `CovalencePlugin` (game-agnostic) | [2] |
| Metadata | `[Info("Name", "Author", "1.0.0")]`, optional `[Description]` | [4][19] |
| Hook method | `private void OnServerInitialized()` style | [13][19] |
| Config file | `oxide/config/<Plugin>.json` | [16] |
| Data files | `oxide/data/` (subfolder per plugin recommended) | [7][17] |
| Lang file | `oxide/lang/<code>/<Plugin>.json` | [7][18] |

Lifecycle sequence [3]:

| Order | Step | Notes |
|-------|------|-------|
| 1 | `Init` | Before dependencies available; exception rolls back |
| 2 | `Loaded` | Read async config/localisation via `Config` |
| 3 | `OnServerInitialized` | Boot nearly complete; runs on hot reload too |
| 4 | `Shutdown` | Only with Advanced Hooks support |
| 5 | `Unload` | After hook routing disabled |

Documented hook examples (Oxide hook pages, 2026-10-08):

| Hook | Signature | Return behaviour | Source |
|------|-----------|------------------|--------|
| `CanLootEntity` | `object CanLootEntity(BasePlayer, WorldItem)` | Non-null overrides default; null proceeds | [12] |
| `OnServerInitialized` | `void OnServerInitialized(bool)` | None | [13] |
| `OnUserPermissionGranted` | `void (string playerId, string permission)` | None | [14] |
| `OnPlayerConnected` | `void (BasePlayer)` | None | [15] |

Oxide hook index category counts (2026-10-08) [11]:

| Category | Hooks | Category | Hooks |
|----------|-------|----------|-------|
| Player | 155 | Server | 46 |
| Entity | 102 | Structure | 33 |
| Item | 64 | Weapon | 25 |
| Vehicle | 52 | Permission | 13 |

Command attributes [4][21]:

| Attribute | Scope | Signature | Framework |
|-----------|-------|-----------|-----------|
| `[ChatCommand]` | Chat | `(BasePlayer, string, string[])` | Oxide [4], Carbon [21] |
| `[ConsoleCommand]` | F1/terminal/RCon | `(ConsoleSystem.Arg)` | Oxide [4], Carbon [21] |
| `[Command]` | Chat and console | Oxide: `(IPlayer, string, string[])`; Carbon: `(BasePlayer, string, string[])` | Oxide [4], Carbon [21] |
| `[Group]`, `[AuthLevel]`, `[Cooldown]`, `[ProtectedCommand]` | Restrictions | n/a | Carbon docs only [21] |

Permission API calls [5][22]:

| Call | Oxide docs | Carbon docs |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| `RegisterPermission(name, plugin)` | Yes [5] | Yes; in `Init()` or `OnServerInitialized()` [22] |
| `UserHasPermission(id, name)` | Yes [5] | Yes [22] |
| `CreateGroup(name, title, rank)` | Yes [5] | Yes; returns false if exists [22] |
| `GetGroupPermissions(group, parents)` | Yes [5] | Yes [22] |
| `AddUserGroup` / `UserHasGroup` | Yes [5] | Not documented on the page [22] |

Naming rules from the Oxide plugin guidelines [8]: commands lowercase with underscores; permissions `pluginname.permission` with lowercase plugin name; locals camelCase; properties PascalCase; semantic versioning with the `[Info]` version updated on every change.

Carbon versus Oxide migration facts, as stated by Carbon [23]:

| Item | Carbon statement |
|------|------------------|
| Coexistence | Oxide and Carbon cannot run on the same install |
| Command prefix | `c.` instead of `o.` |
| Config folder | Oxide `config` becomes `carbon/configs` |
| Plugin source changes | Page does not describe any required |
| Permission storage | Carbon says it uses SQLite-based permissions |

- Carbon "Production Build v2.0.262" was published 2026-10-02 [27].
- Carbon says Harmony 2.0 is used by both frameworks: Carbon has always run it, and Oxide now uses it too [23]. The date Oxide adopted it was not stated.
- Hook counts and signatures track Rust and are volatile; the hook index is regenerated as the framework updates, so re-check pages before relying on a signature [11].

text:
- Treating `Init` as safe for dependencies: the lifecycle page says dependencies are not available in `Init`, and an exception there rolls back compilation [3].
- Config overwritten on unload: some plugins save config when unloaded, so edits made while loaded can be lost; the admin guidance is to unload, edit, load [16].
- Default list entries piling up on restart unless `ObjectCreationHandling.Replace` is set [7].
- Missing `//Requires:` dependency: the plugin will not start [4].
- Returning a value from a hook with documented "No return behavior" has no documented effect; returning non-null from override-style hooks blocks default behaviour [12][13].
- Blocking the main thread with heavy computation or file I/O is called out as disrespectful to the server in the guidelines [8].
- Assuming Carbon and Oxide can be mixed: Carbon states they cannot coexist [23]. Carbon also says it needs unmodified Facepunch DLLs, so Oxide-patched files must be reverted [23].
- Typing `o.` commands on Carbon: they do not work, though aliases can be defined [23].
title: Rust Plugin Development and Hooks

text:
## Guidance 1 — Register permissions early and name them pluginname.action

- **Guidance:** Register every permission in `Init` (or `OnServerInitialized` on Carbon), use lowercase `pluginname.action` names, and gate commands with `[Permission]` rather than hand-written checks where possible.
- **Evidence basis:** Registration in `Init` and the naming convention are documented [2][5][8][22]; the `[Permission]` attribute is documented [4][21].
- **Confidence:** High. Several primary pages from both frameworks agree.
- **So what:** Admins can find and grant the permission with standard commands, and permissions do not collide across plugins.

## Guidance 2 — Keep Init minimal and defer cross-plugin work to OnServerInitialized

- **Guidance:** Do setup that needs other plugins or world state in `OnServerInitialized`, and handle both `true` and `false` values of its parameter so hot reloads behave.
- **Evidence basis:** Init runs before dependencies are available; OnServerInitialized runs on reload with `false` [3][13].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The lifecycle page is clear but the advice is a synthesis, and no primary page tests it.
- **So what:** Fewer load-order bugs when a plugin is reloaded on a live server.

## Guidance 3 — Separate config from data and guard against list accumulation

- **Guidance:** Put admin-tunable settings in the config and plugin-managed state in data files, and set `ObjectCreationHandling.Replace` on default lists.
- **Evidence basis:** Config/data split and the list behaviour [7][16][17].
- **Confidence:** High. Stated on official pages.
- **So what:** Admins edit the right file, backups cover `oxide/data`, and restarts do not duplicate default entries.

## Guidance 4 — Write for Oxide compatibility unless you need Carbon-only features

- **Guidance:** Use `RustPlugin` and `Oxide.Plugins` by default, and use `CarbonPlugin` or Carbon-only command attributes only when you accept losing Oxide portability.
- **Evidence basis:** Carbon documents both shapes and labels Carbon-only attributes [19][21]; Carbon says the plugin structure is the same [28].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Compatibility is the framework's own claim, and the docs do not test every attribute across both.
- **So what:** A single plugin file can serve servers on either framework; test on both before claiming support.

## Guidance 5 — Re-verify every hook signature against the current hook page before shipping

- **Guidance:** Treat a hook's signature and return behaviour as build-specific and check the hook page after each Rust update.
- **Evidence basis:** Oxide shipped a patch for a Rust hotfix and added new hooks the same day [26]; hook pages list the engine call site [12].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The release evidence is two observed releases.
- **So what:** Fewer silently dead hooks after a Rust update.

Resolving it needs the framework core docs or source.

text:
This document goes deeper than the modding foundation on where Rust server plugins come from and on what the marketplaces themselves say about licences, payment, refunds, support and review. The best-documented marketplace is Codefling: its own policy pages state refund, warranty, creator-obligation and curation rules [2][3][4][5][6]. The uMod site, the long-standing free plugin directory, returned HTTP 403 to every direct fetch, so uMod's approval, licence and monetisation rules could not be verified here. This is not legal advice.

Confidence is Low. Codefling claims rest on first-party policy pages and are solid for that one site, but uMod is unread, the other paid sites could not be characterised from their own pages, and the only independent view of the wider market is a single hosting-provider guide. This document does not claim that any named marketplace has hosted a malicious plugin; it records only what named sources say about review and risk.
title: Rust Plugin Marketplaces and Licensing

text:
- Codefling states that creators must make their product licence available before purchase and state limits such as server counts, modifications and redistribution [4].
- Codefling's refund policy says digital purchases are "generally final once a download has been completed", with exceptions for significant unresolved defects, material differences from the description and duplicate or incorrect charges [3].
- Every Codefling file carries a six-month warranty from purchase; Codefling+ purchases get two further years, 30 months in total [5].
- Codefling creators must provide updates and support for paid content for at least six months after first sale [4].
- Codefling's upload guidelines require creators to choose a licence they have the right to apply, forbid DRM, remote kill switches, silent update checks and hidden commands, and say creators handle refund inquiries [16].
- Codefling curators check submissions for malware, harmful code and security issues, but state that approval "is not a guarantee that every defect or risk has been found" [6].
- Oxide's developer guidelines tell plugin authors not to include backdoors, spyware, intentional memory leaks or data miners, and to keep plugins updated after Oxide and game updates [8].
- A hosting provider's 2026 guide lists most free plugins as coming from uMod, and lists paid items from Codefling and chaoscode.io [10].
- Plugins cover the Oxide and Carbon frameworks, which are licensed MIT and GPL-3.0 respectively; those licences cover the frameworks, not individual plugins [11][12].
title: Rust Plugin Marketplaces and Licensing

text: Covered: where plugins are obtained, what the opened marketplace policy pages say about licences, payment, refunds, warranty, support, updates and review, and risks only as documented by named sources. Server-owner view, PC dedicated servers running Oxide or Carbon. Not covered: legal advice or interpretation of any licence, plugin quality reviews, writing plugins (see rust-plugin-development-hooks), the framework comparison (see rust-carbon-vs-oxide), and how a server may charge players (see rust-server-monetisation-guidelines). Policies were read on 2026-10-08 and can change without a Rust patch.
title: Rust Plugin Marketplaces and Licensing

text:
- **Marketplace:** a site where creators list plugins, maps or tools for sale or download. Codefling describes its role as letting creators monetise their work [2].
- **Curation:** Codefling's review of submitted files against its upload guidelines [6].
- **Warranty (Codefling):** a time-limited promise covering significant defects that stop a file performing its advertised functions [5].
- **Product licence:** the creator's own terms for a listing, which Codefling requires to be visible before purchase [4].
title: Rust Plugin Marketplaces and Licensing

text:
**Plugin sources.** A hosting-provider guide published in 2026 sorts popular plugins by source: free plugins such as Vanish, Rust Kits and Gather Manager from uMod; ZombieHorde at $10 from chaoscode.io; and Raidable Bases split into a free base version on uMod and paid premium and prefab base packs on Codefling [10]. That guide calls uMod "the official home of the Oxide ecosystem" and is sold alongside server hosting, so it is not a neutral source [10]. A request to chaoscode.io returned a permanent redirect to rusthq.com, a page titled "RustHQ - Rust Marketplace & Community"; nothing further was readable [13].

**Codefling listing model.** Codefling's front page lists plugins, maps, monuments, prefabs, bases, tools, Discord bots and graphics; each listing shows a price or free marker, seller and rating, and notes dependencies such as Oxide or Carbon [1]. Support is commonly routed to the seller, often via the seller's Discord [1]. A Raid Limits listing carries a "sold as is" wording, showing sellers can attach their own terms [1].

**Licences.** Codefling's registration terms do not set licence terms [7]. Its creator terms require each creator to publish a licence before purchase and state limits on use; licence changes apply only to future purchases, and withdrawing a product or closing an account does not cancel existing buyer licences [4]. Its curation policy tells buyers to check the licence themselves and does not list licence review as a curator check [6]. Creators keep ownership and grant Codefling a non-exclusive licence to host, distribute and promote the content [4].

**Payment and creator rules.** Codefling deducts a sales fee before crediting a creator wallet, but the creator page does not state the percentage; payouts are requested, not automatic, and may be delayed for identity checks, fraud investigation, refunds or chargebacks [4]. Creators must not offer content cheaper elsewhere and must not steer Codefling buyers to buy elsewhere [4].

**Refunds.** Undownloaded purchases are not automatically refundable; after download, refunds may be considered for significant unresolved defects, material differences from the description, duplicate or incorrect charges, or exceptional circumstances; change of mind normally does not qualify [3]. No fixed refund window in days is stated [3]. A refund does not authorise redistribution [3].

**Warranty and support.** The warranty runs six months from purchase, extends to 30 months for purchases made under an active Codefling+ subscription, and continues if the author leaves or stops supporting the file [5]. Buyers contact the author first, then submit a claim if there is no response, the issue stays unresolved or the file appears abandoned [5]. Codefling may assign a new maintainer to an abandoned file, with future proceeds going to that maintainer [4]. Creators must provide updates and support for at least six months after first sale [4].

**Upload guidelines.** Codefling's upload guidelines tell creators to choose a licence they have the right to apply, make its terms available and follow third-party licences; forks need significant changes [16]. Files must not require external licence keys or activation servers, and analytics, tracking, silent update checks and remote kill switches are prohibited [16]. Destructive actions must be documented and need server-owner confirmation, no backdoors or hidden commands are allowed, reviewers may request source code, and mostly AI-generated files are generally not accepted [16]. Creators must list dependencies and extra costs before purchase and are responsible for support and refund inquiries [16].

**Review and removal.** Curators look for malware, harmful code and security issues and test whether a file works as described; some trusted creators can publish before review finishes; a badge shows whether a file has been reviewed [6]. Later versions and later changes to the game, frameworks or dependencies are not covered by an earlier review [6]. A file deemed unacceptable is removed and pre-curation buyers are refunded, but removal does not remove the file from a buyer's server [6].

**Service listings.** Codefling also lists custom-development services. Its page says it does not evaluate, test or guarantee external providers and will not intervene in disputes between customer and provider [9]. One example listing excludes unauthorised code changes and third-party plugin issues from support [9].

**Disclaimer.** Codefling advises users to read instructions and back up data and configuration before installing or updating files, and limits its responsibility for third-party content to the extent permitted by law [14].

**Authoring norms from the framework.** Oxide's plugin guidelines say developers should avoid code that could harm the server or players, including backdoors, spyware, intentional memory leaks and data miners, and should tell users if adapting to an update will take time [8]. Its best-practice guide advises validating input and keeping dependencies updated, and says nothing on plugin licensing [15].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Read the creator's licence on the listing before buying, because curation does not check it

- **Guidance:** Before paying for a plugin, read the product licence on the listing and ask the creator about multi-server use, modification and redistribution if the licence is silent.
- **Evidence basis:** Creators must disclose licence limits before purchase [4]; the curation policy does not list licence review and tells buyers to check [6].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Both statements are first-party policy text, but they describe one marketplace only.
- **So what:** Keep a record of the licence text at the time of purchase, since changes apply only to future purchases [4].

## Guidance 2 — Test downloads on staging and keep backups, because review is not a guarantee

- **Guidance:** Install new or updated plugins on a staging server first and back up data and configuration, regardless of marketplace badges.
- **Evidence basis:** Codefling says approval is not a guarantee and does not cover later versions [6]; it advises backups before installing [14]; Oxide warns that updates can break plugins [8].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The reasoning is straightforward but the sources are vendor statements; no named incident is cited here.
- **So what:** A removed or flagged file can still be on your server, so you may need to undo its changes yourself [6].

## Guidance 3 — Claim refunds or warranty early and through the right channel

- **Guidance:** Report defects soon after purchase, contact the author first, and only then use the warranty claim route.
- **Evidence basis:** Refund policy asks for prompt contact [3]; the warranty runs from purchase date and requires author contact first [5].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Written procedure from one marketplace; outcomes in practice are not evidenced.
- **So what:** Collect version, errors and reproduction steps before the six months lapse [5].

## Guidance 4 — Do not generalise Codefling terms to other sites

- **Guidance:** Treat each marketplace as having its own refund, licence and support terms, and read them separately.
- **Evidence basis:** Codefling's rules are specific to its pages [3][4][5]; the other sources found give no comparable terms [10][13].
- **Confidence:** Low. This rests on absence of evidence for sites that could not be read.

text:
This deep-dive covers how a Rust server operator polices a server: the console commands for admins and moderators, local bans, the centralized ban API, the secure-server state as Facepunch describes it, and the cheating clauses of Facepunch's server guidelines. It goes deeper than rust-server-administration-foundation and does not repeat the convar tables in rust-server-convars-reference.

Confidence is Medium. Command, ban API and guideline facts are first-party Facepunch text and are well supported. Facepunch deliberately discloses little about how Easy Anti-Cheat (EAC) detects cheats, so the anti-cheat picture is built from devblog statements only, and the secure-server statistics come from a small sample. Checked against the October 2026 update [9].
title: Rust Moderation and Anti-Cheat

text:
- Admin commands `ban`, `banid`, `unban`, `kick`, `mute`, `moderatorid` and `ownerid` are documented on Facepunch's Useful Console Commands page [2].
- A kick lets the player rejoin immediately; a ban is what prevents rejoining [2].
- Centralized banning checks an HTTP API when a player joins, supports mutes as well as bans, and does not kick players already connected [1].
- Facepunch's guidelines state that cheating, griefing or hacking is strictly prohibited, and breaches can mean delisting, other sanctions or a game ban [3].
- The guidelines do not name EAC or any anti-cheat tool [3]; Facepunch devblogs do name EAC [7][10][11].
- Servers can opt in to requiring TPM and Secure Boot (announced 5 March 2026) [7]; Facepunch reported about 1 in 63 players as cheaters on its secure servers against 1 in 42 on regular servers [8].
- Facepunch reported 338,000+ total bans and 296,000+ permanent bans applied in 2025 [10].
- `server.listplayerreportcounts` lets admins see how many reports players have received (7 August 2025) [5].
title: Rust Moderation and Anti-Cheat

text: Covers vanilla Rust dedicated servers on PC: moderator tooling, banning, the centralized ban endpoint, Facepunch's stated secure-server and EAC position, and the guidelines on cheating. Not covered: plugin-based admin tools (see rust-modding-plugins-foundation and rust-plugin-development-hooks), the full convar table for secure servers (see rust-server-convars-reference), in-game combat rules (see rust-combat-damage-model), and any description of how cheats work or how EAC detects them, which Facepunch does not publish. Console editions are excluded.
title: Rust Moderation and Anti-Cheat

text:
- **Auth level** — admin tier: owner is level 2, moderator is level 1 [2][4].
- **Centralized banning** — an optional external ban list queried over HTTP at join time [1].
- **EAC** — Easy Anti-Cheat, the anti-cheat partner Facepunch names in its devblogs [10][11].
- **Secure server** — a server that meets Facepunch's secure criteria to appear in the client browser, including a minimum encryption level [6].
- **Secure tag** — browser tag for servers requiring TPM and Secure Boot for all players [7].
- **Premium server** — a Facepunch server that requires a Steam inventory valued at $15 or more [10].
title: Rust Moderation and Anti-Cheat

text:
**Granting authority.** Run `users` to find a SteamID, then `ownerid` or `moderatorid`. The player must reconnect to receive the level, and the change saves automatically. Admins can also be written into `users.cfg` in the `server.identity/cfg/` folder, but only while the server is shut down [4]. `removeowner` and `removemoderator` revoke the levels [2].

**Command set.** `ban` takes a Steam64 ID, name, reason and optional duration written like `1M7d5m`; `banid` bans a Steam64 ID even when the player is not on the server; `unban` removes a ban; `bans` and `banlistex` list bans; `kick` removes a player who can rejoin immediately. `mute` and `unmute` act locally for a player and server-wide when used by an admin. `killplayer`, `resetstate`, `combatlog <Steam64ID>`, `players`, `playerlist`, `status` (includes IP address and time played) and `users` support investigations [2].

**Centralized banning.** The operator hosts the web service because Facepunch does not provide one. Setting `server.bansServerEndpoint` makes the server request `GET /api/rustBans/{steamID64}` when a player joins, adding a trailing `/` if the endpoint does not end in `/` or `=`. A 2xx response must carry JSON with `steamId`, `reason`, `expiryDate` (Unix timestamp; zero or negative is permanent) and `isMute`; 404 means not banned; any other status is a failure. `server.bansServerFailureMode` 0 lets players join on failure and 1 rejects them; `server.bansServerTimeout` defaults to 5 seconds. Changing these needs no restart, and bans do not kick connected players, so use `kick` for that [1].

**Guidelines on cheating.** The Community Server and Hosting Guidelines (updated 15 July 2025) say cheating, griefing or hacking is strictly prohibited. Failure to comply may lead to delisting from the server browser or other sanctions, and serious or repeated breach may lead to a game ban. Community servers are at Facepunch's discretion, and the operator is responsible for the server [3]. The guidelines do not mention EAC [3].

**Secure-server state.** On 7 August 2025 Facepunch told operators to use the `-insecure` startup parameter instead of setting `server.secure` false, and added a minimum encryption requirement for appearing in the client browser [5]. On 4 September 2025 the minimum became level 2, which is already the default for dedicated servers, and `server.secure` was slated for removal [6]. On 5 March 2026 servers gained an opt-in requirement for TPM and Secure Boot, which Facepunch said lets EAC work better; servers requiring both for all players get a Secure tag, and per-account requirements use a separate convar without the tag [7]. Convar names and defaults are in rust-server-convars-reference.

- Expecting `kick` to be a sanction: the kicked player can rejoin immediately [2].
- Setting `server.secure false`: Facepunch moved insecure servers to `-insecure` [5][6].

title: Rust Moderation and Anti-Cheat

text:
## Guidance 1 — Pair every ban with a kick and keep a written reason

- **Guidance:** When banning an online player, run the ban and then `kick`, and always supply a reason and duration.
- **Evidence basis:** Bans (including centralized ones) do not remove players already connected, and `kick` is the removal command [1][2]; the ban command accepts a reason and duration [2].
- **Confidence:** High. Both behaviours are stated on first-party wiki pages.
- **So what:** A ban alone can leave the offender playing until they disconnect.

## Guidance 2 — Treat centralized banning as shared infrastructure

- **Guidance:** Only run a centralized ban endpoint that is fast and monitored, and choose the failure mode deliberately.
- **Evidence basis:** The check happens at join time with a 5 second default timeout, failure mode 0 admits and 1 rejects players, and Facepunch advises fast APIs [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The mechanics are documented, but which mode suits a given community is a judgement.
- **So what:** Fail-open keeps a server joinable but lets banned players in during an outage; fail-closed does the reverse.

## Guidance 3 — Do not rely on secure mode alone to stop cheating

- **Guidance:** Treat TPM and Secure Boot enforcement as one deterrent alongside active moderation and reporting, and weigh the population cost.
- **Evidence basis:** Facepunch measured about 1 in 63 cheaters on secure servers against 1 in 42 on regular ones from only six servers, and said about 60% of players have the required features [8]; it described the effect as less than premium servers [8].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Primary source, but a small sample and an operator's own outcomes may differ.
- **So what:** Secure servers have fewer cheaters, not none, and fewer eligible players.

## Guidance 4 — Write your own rules with the guidelines in mind

- **Guidance:** Publish server rules that match the guidelines' prohibition on cheating, griefing and hacking, and do not present your server as official.
- **Evidence basis:** The guidelines prohibit them, make operators responsible for their servers, and allow delisting, sanctions or a game ban [3].
- **Confidence:** High. This restates Facepunch's own text; whether a rule suits your community is up to you.
- **So what:** Clear rules help justify bans and reduce exposure to sanctions.
title: Rust Moderation and Anti-Cheat

text:
This document is the entry point for running a Rust dedicated server: installing it through SteamCMD, opening ports, choosing launch parameters, using `server.cfg`, generating a map, wiping on schedule, administering through RCON and auth levels, and staying inside Facepunch's server guidelines. It stays at overview depth and points to the Facepunch wiki pages that hold the detail.

Confidence is Medium. Most install, port, wipe and ban facts come from the Facepunch wiki and Facepunch's own guidelines and devblogs, which are primary. However, several wiki pages are old or thin (RCON, convar defaults and anti-cheat configuration are not documented in the pages read), so those areas are stated narrowly and flagged as open questions. Checked against the October 2026 update [8].
title: Rust Server Administration: Foundation

text:
- The Rust dedicated server is Steam app id 258550, installed with SteamCMD using an anonymous login [1].
- The game port is UDP 28015 by default, the query port is UDP and must differ from the game port, and RCON is TCP [1].
- `server.cfg` lives in `rust/server/server.identity/cfg/`, is read at startup, overrides command-line settings, and is never rewritten by the server [1].
- The default wipe schedule is the first Thursday of the month at 19:00 London time, aligned with Facepunch forced wipes [2].
- `ownerid` grants auth level 2 and `moderatorid` grants auth level 1 [7].
- Facepunch's Community Server and Hosting Guidelines (updated 15 July 2025) permit several monetisation methods but forbid granting Facepunch DLC to players who do not own it [3].
- Servers can require TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot; Facepunch reported fewer cheaters on its secure servers [9][8].
- A mandatory server and client update was announced for 22 October 2026 at 18:00 BST [8].
title: Rust Server Administration: Foundation

text: Covers vanilla dedicated servers on PC (Windows and Linux) as documented by Facepunch, at overview level, against the October 2026 build. Not covered: console editions, Oxide/Carbon plugin installation (see rust-modding-plugins-foundation), in-game mechanics (rust-game-mechanics-foundation), crafting data (rust-items-crafting-foundation), building and raiding rules (rust-building-raiding-foundation) and patch history (rust-updates-meta-foundation). Hosting-provider panels and third-party tooling are out of scope.
title: Rust Server Administration: Foundation

text:
- **SteamCMD** — Valve's command-line Steam client used to download the server files [1].
- **server identity** — a named folder holding one server's saves, config and admin files, so one install can run several servers [5].
- **Auth level** — admin permission tier: 2 owner, 1 moderator [7].
- **RCON** — remote console used to run server commands over the network [1].
- **Forced wipe** — Facepunch's monthly update-day wipe that a new protocol version makes necessary [2][5].
title: Rust Server Administration: Foundation

text:
**Install.** The server app id is 258550. The wiki gives the Linux form `./steamcmd.sh +force_install_dir ../rust +login anonymous +app_update 258550 validate +quit`. Omitting `+login` yields "No subscription". Beta branches are installed with `-beta <branch>` (for example `staging`). After testing a higher build, return to the `public` branch or delete the steamapps folder [1].

**Ports.** `server.port` (UDP, default 28015) and `server.queryport` (UDP) must both be open. If `queryport` is unset it defaults to one more than the higher of `server.port` or `rcon.port`, and it must differ from `server.port`. `rcon.port` is TCP and Rust+ also uses a TCP port; RCON and Rust+ ports are needed only if those features are wanted [1].

**Launch parameters and server.cfg.** Common launch arguments are `-batchmode`, `+server.port`, `+server.level "Procedural Map"`, `+server.seed`, `+server.worldsize`, `+server.maxplayers`, `+server.ip`, `+rcon.port`, `+rcon.password`, `+rcon.web 1` and `-logfile`. `server.cfg` takes the same settings without the `+`/`-` prefix, is read at start-up, overrides the command line, and is never edited by the server itself. Some variables (for example weather chance settings) can only be set once the server is running [1]. The command `server.writecfg` writes current convars to the cfg files [7].

**Map generation.** The wiki describes procedural maps with a seed (0 to 2147483647) and world size (the wiki suggests 1000 to 6000; larger maps need more disk and memory) [1]. Procedural maps are saved as `proceduralmap.SIZE.SEED.map` [5]. A JSON file loaded with `+world.configfile` can switch off roads, rivers, powerlines and underwater labs or blacklist/whitelist prefabs; it applies only when a map is first generated, so existing maps need the `.map` file deleted [4].

**Saves and wipes.** The `.sav` file holds entities, buildings and deployables, and the protocol number in its name increases at a forced wipe so the server starts a new file; a blueprint wipe also requires deleting `player.blueprints` [5]. The wipe timer defaults to the first Thursday monthly at 19:00 London time, with weekly and biweekly options, controlled by `wipetimer.wipeDayofWeek`, `wipetimer.wipeHourofDay`, `wipetimer.wipeTimezone`, `wipetimer.wipeUnixTimestampOverride` and `wipetimer.wipeCronOverride`; the `PrintWipe` command shows the calculated schedule [2].

**Administration.** `users` lists players with Steam64 IDs; `ownerid <steamid> "<name>"` and `moderatorid <steamid> "<name>"` grant auth levels 2 and 1; `removeowner` revokes level 2; the player must reconnect to receive the level [1][7]. `kick` and `ban` (with optional duration such as `1M7d5m`) are available to admins [7]. An optional centralized ban list is enabled by pointing `server.bansServerEndpoint` at a self-hosted HTTP API; it blocks joins but does not kick players already online [6].

**Rules and anti-cheat.** Facepunch's guidelines allow a server fee or subscription, donations, cosmetics and enhancements, a server currency, and adverts or sponsorships. Facepunch DLC must be available to players who own it and must not be granted to those who do not; only test servers are excepted. Enforcement can include delisting, other sanctions or a game ban, and cheating, griefing or hacking are prohibited [3]. The guidelines name no specific anti-cheat tool [3]. Facepunch announced that servers can require TPM and Secure Boot [8][9].

text:
- Omitting `+login anonymous` makes SteamCMD fail with "No subscription" [1].
- Running SteamCMD from a startup script reverts Oxide files to vanilla; Oxide must be reinstalled after each update [1].
- The server never writes `server.cfg`, so changes made at runtime are lost unless written with `server.writecfg` [1][7].
- Renaming an old `.sav` to dodge a forced wipe is called dangerous and ill-advised by the wiki [5].
- Map generation settings do not affect an existing map; delete the `.map` file to regenerate [4].
- Banning through the centralized list does not remove players already connected; use `kick` [6].
- Reducing Tier0 topology too far can leave a map with no spawn points [4].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Keep the wipe schedule at its default unless you have a reason

- **Guidance:** Leave the wipe timer on the default first-Thursday 19:00 London schedule and use the override convars only for deliberate off-cycle wipes.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki says the default aligns with forced wipes and rarely needs changing [2], and the save filename protocol changes at forced wipes [5].
- **Confidence:** High. Both statements are first-party Facepunch documentation.
- **So what:** A schedule that disagrees with the forced wipe invites a mid-cycle wipe or a broken save.

## Guidance 2 — Re-check launch arguments and convars after every monthly update

- **Guidance:** After each update, read the devblog server section and re-test launch arguments and `server.cfg` before opening the server to players.
- **Evidence basis:** Convars were added, changed and removed in consecutive updates [8][9], and the install page flags outdated content [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The pattern is documented, but how often a given setting breaks is inference.
- **So what:** Reading the notes avoids silent behaviour changes and covers the announced 22 October mandatory update [8].

## Guidance 3 — Decide monetisation and DLC policy before launch

- **Guidance:** If you sell anything, keep to the listed methods and never unlock Facepunch DLC for non-owners.
- **Evidence basis:** The guidelines list permitted methods and the DLC prohibition, with enforcement up to a game ban [3].
- **Confidence:** High. The source is Facepunch's own legal text, though only the live page is authoritative.
- **So what:** Breaching it risks delisting or bans for the operator.

## Guidance 4 — Weigh secure mode and set a strong RCON password

- **Guidance:** Evaluate TPM and Secure Boot requirements as a cheat deterrent, accepting that a share of players cannot meet them, and never leave the placeholder RCON password.
- **Evidence basis:** Facepunch's figures show fewer cheaters on secure servers but only about 60% of players qualifying [9]; the wiki tells admins to change the RCON password [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The cheater figure comes from a six-server sample reported by Facepunch.
- **So what:** Stricter entry trades population for fewer cheaters.

title: Rust Server Convars Reference

text:
This reference lists the server convars that Facepunch itself documents or names, grouped by purpose: startup and world, decay and upkeep, Rust+ companion, secure-server and encryption, tags and gamemodes, and recent devblog additions. It goes deeper than rust-server-administration-foundation by giving names, defaults and effects row by row, and by resolving the foundation's open question on secure-server convars.

Confidence is Medium. Every row comes from a Facepunch wiki page or devblog, but Facepunch publishes no complete convar list, many pages are marked as old or work in progress, and several defaults are simply not stated. Gather-rate convars and the RCON connection-limit convar names were not found on any Facepunch page and are listed as gaps rather than guessed. Checked against the October 2026 update [6].
title: Rust Server Convars Reference

text:
- Facepunch's wiki documents only a handful of decay convars: `decay.scale` (default 1), `decay.upkeep_period_minutes` (default 1440) and `decay.upkeep_grief_protection` (default 1440) [1].
- `server.useServerWideRequiredSystemConfig` requires TPM and Secure Boot for all players and earns the Secure browser tag; `server.usePerPlayerRequiredSystemConfig` enforces per player and does not earn the tag [8].
- `server.secure` was removed on 4 September 2025; insecure servers now pass `-insecure` at startup, and a secure server needs `server.encryption` set to 2 [9][10].
- `app.port` defaults to the larger of game port or RCON port plus 67 (28082 with default ports), must be 10000 or higher, and `-1` disables Rust+ [3].
- `rcon.port` is TCP and `server.queryport` is UDP and must differ from `server.port` [5].
- `UsePlayerUpdateJobs` has defaulted to 2 since the April 2026 update [7].
- No Facepunch page opened for this document lists a gather-rate convar or any default for one *(gap, see Open Questions)*.
- The Useful Console Commands page says it is a work in progress and last updated "A Long Time Ago" [1].
title: Rust Server Convars Reference

text: Covers vanilla dedicated-server variables on PC that appear on Facepunch wiki pages or Facepunch devblogs, checked against the October 2026 update. Convars are set on the command line with a `+` prefix or in `server.cfg` without it, or discovered via `find` in the server console [5]. Not covered: Oxide/Carbon plugin configuration (see rust-modding-plugins-foundation and rust-plugin-development-hooks), client-only convars, third-party host panels, and community-maintained convar dumps, which were not used.
title: Rust Server Convars Reference

text:
- **Convar** — a console variable or command that configures the server; set at launch, in `server.cfg`, or at runtime [5].
- **Upkeep** — resources a Tool Cupboard consumes to protect a base from decay [2].
- **Secure tag** — server-browser tag shown only when TPM and Secure Boot are enforced for all players [8].
- **Companion server** — the Rust+ listener configured with the `app.*` convars [3].
title: Rust Server Convars Reference

text:
**Setting convars.** Launch arguments use `+name value`; `server.cfg` in `server/<identity>/cfg/` takes the same settings without the prefix. For settings not in the wiki table the page suggests the `find` console command, for example `find image` [5]. The foundation document covers file locations and precedence.

**Decay and upkeep.** A Tool Cupboard pays upkeep, described as a fraction of the resources used to build, per 24 hours. With no resources in a cupboard, decay starts immediately. Decay starts at the outermost exposed pieces and moves inward, and if one upkeep material runs out only parts of that material decay [2]. After upkeep runs out, the wiki gives full-decay times: twig 1 hour, wood 3 hours, stone 5 hours, metal 8 hours, armoured 12 hours. A destroyed cupboard that held resources consumes up to 24 hours of upkeep, protecting the base for that long [2]. The tool-cupboard page names no convars and carries no build date [2]; the console-commands page supplies the three decay convars [1]. Vehicle decay is separate: minicopter, attack and transport helicopters have their own inside and outside decay timers [1].

**Rust+ companion.** `app.port` sets the listening port and `-1` disables Rust+ (on the command line this is written `+app.port 1-` because of parser conflicts). The server must reach companion-rust.facepunch.com. `app.listenip` selects the NIC, `app.publicip` sets the address the app uses when `app.info` shows a wrong one, and `app.id` carries a warning not to change it [3].

**Secure servers and encryption.** From 5 March 2026 servers can opt in to requiring TPM and Secure Boot [8]. From 7 August 2025 an insecure server is started with `-insecure` rather than `server.secure false` [9]; on 4 September 2025 Facepunch removed `server.secure` and required `server.encryption` 2 for a server to count as secure [10]. The pages opened do not mention Easy Anti-Cheat settings [6][8][9][10].

**Tags and gamemodes.** `server.tags` takes a comma-separated list (example `weekly,vanilla,roleplay`), `server.pve` applies the PvE tag, up to four tags show at once, and tags in the same group should not be combined [11]. `server.gamemode` sets a gamemode at startup, empty meaning default gameplay [4].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Treat the wiki convar defaults as starting points and verify with `find`

- **Guidance:** Before relying on any default in this table, confirm the live value with the server console `find` command after each monthly update.
- **Evidence basis:** The console-commands page is work in progress and old [1], the wiki itself recommends `find` for unlisted settings [5], and convars change monthly [6][7].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The staleness of the pages is documented; how many defaults have drifted is not known.
- **So what:** Avoids trusting a stale default when tuning decay or ports.

## Guidance 2 — Change decay with `decay.scale` first

- **Guidance:** To make a server more or less punishing about decay, adjust `decay.scale` before touching the upkeep period, and record any change in the server description.
- **Evidence basis:** `decay.scale` is the single documented multiplier, while the upkeep convars shift only cost timing and grief protection [1]; material decay times are documented separately [2].
- **Confidence:** Low. The ordering is inference, and the effect of the scale on each material time is not documented.
- **So what:** A single multiplier is easier to reason about and revert than three interacting values.

## Guidance 3 — Use server-wide secure enforcement only if you accept the population cost

- **Guidance:** Enable `server.useServerWideRequiredSystemConfig` only if reduced cheating matters more than losing players without TPM and Secure Boot.
- **Evidence basis:** Enforcement and the tag are documented [8], and Facepunch reported that roughly 60% of players have the features enabled [7].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The mechanism is first-party; the trade-off is judgement.
- **So what:** Expect a smaller pool of eligible players in return for the Secure tag.

title: Rust Server Monetisation and Hosting Guidelines

text:
This document reads Facepunch's Community Server and Hosting Guidelines for people who run Rust servers. It covers what the policy says about charging players, donations, cosmetics, server currency and adverts, the rule about Facepunch DLC, the duty not to pose as official, and the stated consequences of a breach. It is a reading of the policy, not legal advice; only the live page is authoritative.

Confidence is Medium. The permitted methods, the DLC rules and the sanctions come straight from Facepunch's own page and are well sourced. But several things people ask about are not in the policy at all: there is no pay-to-win definition, no logo or trademark clause, and no rules aimed at hosting companies. Where this document discusses those gaps it relies on community writing and says so.
title: Rust Server Monetisation and Hosting Guidelines

text:
- The guidelines were last updated 15 July 2025 and are the page the Administration foundation already points to [1].
- Facepunch says servers may be monetised, with five examples: a fee or subscription, donations, cosmetic items, effects or enhancements, a server currency, and adverts, sponsorships or product placements [1].
- Players who validly bought Facepunch DLC must be able to access it on all servers, and servers may not give Facepunch DLC to non-owners or bypass ownership checks [1].
- Servers may restrict non-Facepunch content such as custom or Workshop content [1].
- A server must be clearly unofficial and must not pretend to be Facepunch [1].
- Breach may lead to delisting from the server browser or other sanctions; serious or repeated breach may lead to a game ban [1].
- The text read for this document does not contain the words pay-to-win, logo, trademark or reseller, and "hosting" appears only in the page title [1].
- The claim that queue skip is the only permitted monetisation appears in a store vendor blog [4] and is not supported by the policy's own list [1] *(assessed)*.

text: Covers the Facepunch policy as it applies to Rust PC community servers, as read on 8 October 2026. Plugin sales are touched on only through Facepunch's separate Modding Guidelines [2]. Not covered: payment processor terms, store platform rules, consumer law, tax, or the contract between a customer and a hosting company. For admin mechanics see rust-server-administration-foundation; for cosmetics see rust-skins-cosmetics.
title: Rust Server Monetisation and Hosting Guidelines

text:
- **Community Server** — a private, unofficial server run by someone other than Facepunch [1].
- **Facepunch DLC** — paid Facepunch content, including approved in-game purchases, which owners must be able to use on any server [1].
- **Delisting** — removal from the in-game server browser, the first sanction the policy names [1].
- **Queue skip** — a paid priority-entry perk sold by many servers; not mentioned in the policy text [1][3].
title: Rust Server Monetisation and Hosting Guidelines

text:
**Permission to run servers.** The policy permits private, unofficial and community servers provided the operator follows the guidelines, labels the server fairly to players and obeys the law [1].

**Monetisation.** Under the question "Am I allowed to monetise my Servers" the answer is yes "for example" by a single fee or subscription, donations, "cosmetic items, effects or enhancements", the operator's own server currency, and adverts, sponsorships or product placements [1]. The list is introduced as examples [1]; a practitioner reading treats it as illustrative rather than exhaustive [3].

**DLC.** Three rules apply. Facepunch DLC bought validly must be accessible on all servers. Non-Facepunch content, including custom or Steam Workshop content, may be restricted. A server may not grant Facepunch DLC to players who have not bought it. Servers set up to test game mechanics may temporarily grant or restrict Facepunch DLC for testing only [1].

**Server requirements.** The operator must make clear the server is unofficial; is responsible for compliance and for third parties using the server; must not run illegal activity, circumvent paid content, harm the games or players, infringe rights or carry malware; and must keep content and adverts suitable for the games' target audience. Cheating, griefing and hacking are prohibited. Operators may distribute their server but not the game or paid Facepunch content [1].

**Discretion and precedence.** Facepunch states that the ability to create, use and distribute servers is at its discretion and can be withdrawn, particularly to protect Facepunch or its games. The Terms of Service and Privacy Policy override the guidelines on conflict, and updates bind once posted [1].

**Enforcement.** The page says failure to comply "may result in delisting from the server browser or other sanctions", that serious or repeated breach may result in a game ban, and that a breach may also breach the Terms of Service [1].

**Related modding rules.** Facepunch's separate Modding Guidelines (last updated 28 August 2019) let a creator sell a mod they own and forbid presenting a mod as official [2].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Treat the DLC rule as the hard line and design around it

- **Guidance:** Never grant Facepunch DLC or Marketplace skins to non-owners and never lock owners out of DLC they bought; check any skin plugin for this before enabling it.
- **Evidence basis:** The policy states both DLC rules and names delisting and game bans as sanctions [1]; a practitioner identifies skin plugins as the main practical risk [3].
- **Confidence:** High. The rules are explicit first-party text; only the plugin risk is practitioner opinion.
- **So what:** Selling skin access behind a rank is the product most likely to cost you your listing.

## Guidance 2 — Do not rely on queue skip being the only allowed product

- **Guidance:** Plan your store against the policy's own list, not against vendor claims that only queue skip is allowed.
- **Evidence basis:** The policy lists five example methods [1]; one article says queue skip is typically the only option [4]; another says the policy never mentions it [3].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The policy text is clear but Facepunch has not publicly ruled on specific products.
- **So what:** You have wider latitude than some vendors say, but discretion lies with Facepunch [1].

## Guidance 3 — Define pay-to-win yourself and publish it

- **Guidance:** Because the policy neither defines nor bans pay-to-win, state publicly what your ranks and kits do, and keep gameplay advantages modest if you want player trust.
- **Evidence basis:** No pay-to-win text and an undefined "enhancements" [1]; a practitioner advises stating what ranks do [3]; the policy requires fair labelling [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The absence of a rule is documented, but the trust advice is community opinion.
- **So what:** Fair labelling is the only stated standard, so clear descriptions protect you against complaints and breach claims.

## Guidance 4 — Keep official-looking branding off your server

- **Guidance:** Do not use names, banners or descriptions that suggest the server is run by Facepunch; for any use of Facepunch logos, ask Facepunch's legal contact first.
- **Evidence basis:** The policy bars posing as Facepunch and is silent on logos [1]; the Modding Guidelines also bar presenting a mod as official [2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The official-status rule is explicit; the logo advice is a cautious inference from silence.
- **So what:** Silence is not permission, and the policy lets Facepunch withdraw server permission at its discretion [1].

title: Rust Server Performance

text:
This deep-dive goes below the overview in rust-server-administration-foundation and covers what Facepunch documents about running a Rust server fast: hardware and operating-system requirements, the profiler and measurement commands, the performance-related convars Facepunch has named in devblogs, and what recent updates changed in server threading, allocation and entity networking.

Confidence is Medium. The hardware floor, the profiler and the devblog convars are first-party. But Facepunch's wiki gives no CPU figure, no entity-count limit, and no documentation of tick rate, garbage-collection or save-interval convars in any page opened for this document. Those topics rest on hosting-provider articles, which are labelled practitioner evidence and conflict with each other. Checked against the October 2026 update [5].
title: Rust Server Performance

text:
- Facepunch's wiki lists 12 GB free RAM (more for a 6k map), 15 GB free disk (SSD/NVMe highly preferred) and Windows, Linux or OSX, and says these values "are not fixed and highly depend on the use case and population of the server" [1].
- The wiki states no CPU figure, only that more players need a faster CPU [1].
- The server has a built-in profiler enabled with the `-enableProfiler` launch argument; leaving it enabled slightly decreases performance [2].
- `UsePlayerUpdateJobs` defaults to 2 since the Spring Clean update, with level 3 experimental [4].
- Livestock budgets NPC processing per frame, so NPCs react slower under load instead of the server slowing down [5].
- Practitioner guides disagree on the fps and tick values to use and on the GC buffer convar name, and none of those settings was found in Facepunch documentation *(assessed)* [10][11][12].
title: Rust Server Performance

text: Covers PC dedicated servers (Windows and Linux) running vanilla or modded, checked against the October 2026 update. Hardware, operating system, measurement, tick and frame-rate convars, garbage collection, saving, entity load and the update history of server optimisations. Not covered: general convar listings (rust-server-convars-reference), plugin-specific profiling (rust-plugin-development-hooks, rust-carbon-vs-oxide), hosting-provider pricing and console editions.
title: Rust Server Performance

text:
- **Server FPS** — the server's frame rate, readable with the `fps` command on the server [3].
- **`fps.limit`** — maximum frame rate; the `sv` prefix targets the server [3].
- **Garbage collection (GC)** — automatic memory reclamation in the Unity runtime; allocation pressure on it is a stated Facepunch concern [6].
- **Entity** — any networked object such as buildings, deployables, NPCs and vehicles; see rust-building-raiding-foundation.
- **Practitioner evidence** — advice from hosting providers, not Facepunch.
title: Rust Server Performance

text:
**Requirements.** The wiki's Requirements list is an OS "based on Windows, Linux or OSX", 12 GB free RAM ("6k map will use more") and 15 GB free disk with SSD/NVMe highly preferred; it links two third-party RAM calculators and stresses the values are not fixed [1]. Map size (`+server.worldsize`, 1000 to 6000) raises disk and memory need, and more players (`+server.maxplayers`) need a faster CPU [1]. The Linux console is not interactive, so an RCON client or a screen session is needed [1].

**Networking threading.** The wiki notes the query port was changed in the 2 February 2023 update to support the new multi-threaded networking, described as a performance benefit [1].

**Measurement.** `fps` returns the current frames per second on client or server; `fps.limit` sets the maximum frame rate, with the `sv` prefix for the server; `perf 0` to `perf 6` show stats, with RAM usage at level 3, invokes at 5 and tasks at 6; `benchmark` runs a simulation of many parts of the game [3]. The profiler starts with `-enableProfiler`. `profile.perfsnapshot [delay] [name] [frames]` records 1 to 10 frames; `profile.perfsnapshot_stream` records until a buffer of up to 256 MB fills. Recording can noticeably slow the server, a snapshot must finish saving before another starts or the server can crash, and snapshots are saved as `.json.gz` in the `profiler` folder, openable in Perfetto [2].

**Threaded player updates.** In Spring Clean Facepunch set `UsePlayerUpdateJobs` to 2 by default, with the 0 and 1 modes slated for removal; level 3 is experimental and uses UniTask to reduce allocations and parallelise anti-hack and network streaming [4]. A later post says level 3 skips NetWrite preallocation and "can save 0.6ms on busy frames" [6]. Livestock lists a level 4 (experimental) fix for syncvar serialisation thread safety [5].

**Allocation and GC pressure.** The Built Different pool rewrite is described as "vital for avoiding creating pressure on the Garbage Collector"; it removed or amortised about 20 allocation sources on the server, and servers can revert the new lock-free pool with `pool.usemutexpool 1` [6]. Spring Clean added lazy allocation of Network.Group internals and dynamic minimum capacity for object work queues [4].

**Entity networking and processing.** Spring Clean networks entities in a large blocky circle rather than a square, with per-entity network ranges so small items load only when near [4]. Livestock processes only a subset of NPCs per frame up to a hardcoded time budget, parallelises vehicle ticking and reports navigation performance at least doubled [5]. Built Different caps the time of a single pathfinding query [6].

**Industrial and decay load.** The Industrial update added `server.conveyorMoveFrequency`, `server.industrialCrafterFrequency` and `server.maxItemStacksMovedPerTickIndustrial` [7]. Devblog 115 added `decay.tick` to scale decay to a server's wipe schedule, `maxflood` for the player-tick flood threshold, and `noclip_protection` mode 3 with `noclip_stepsize` and `noclip_maxsteps` [9].

**Historic baseline.** In 2015 Facepunch reported servers under 5 fps, traced to rigidbody use, `IsInvoking` and moving the player on every tick, with a feedback loop where a dropped frame rate could not recover [8].

**Practitioner layer (not Facepunch).** Hosting guides describe `server.tickrate` as read at startup with 30 to 60 as a range [10][12], `fps.limit` values (30 in one config table [11]; 30 to 60 [10]; 120 under a different name [12]), `gc.buffer` 256 [11], `server.saveinterval` 300 [11][12], restarts every 12 to 24 hours [12], and single-thread clock speed outweighing core count [10][13]. These are labelled hosting-provider advice.

text:
- 1 October 2026 (Livestock): per-frame NPC budget, parallel vehicle ticking, doubled navigation performance, a fix for leaked SyncVar buffers with parallel saves, and a level 4 jobs fix [5].
- Built Different (reported by a practitioner as 4 June 2026 [10]): pool rewrite, about 20 server allocation sources removed, `pool.usemutexpool` fallback, `UsePlayerUpdateJobs 3` NetWrite saving, pathfinding time cap [6].

text:
- Leaving `-enableProfiler` on in production: Facepunch says it slightly decreases performance until the argument is removed [2].
- Starting a second snapshot before the first has saved can crash the server [2].
- Treating the wiki RAM figure as a fixed requirement; the page says it is not [1].
- Copying convar names from hosting guides, which disagree (`gc.buffer` versus `gc.buffercount`, `fps.limit` versus `server.fpslimit`) [10][11][12].
- Assuming a hosting plan tier is a sizing rule; plan RAM on provider pages is a product tier [10][13].

text:
- Plugins add load that profiler snapshots can show; see rust-plugin-development-hooks and rust-carbon-vs-oxide [2].
- Map size and wipe cadence affect memory and file size; see rust-wipes-map-generation and rust-server-convars-reference [1].
- Entities from industrial, electricity and turret systems add per-tick work; see rust-electricity-logic and rust-turrets-deployables [7].
- NPC and animal load is budgeted per frame; see rust-wildlife-npcs [5].
- Anti-hack and network streaming are part of the threaded player update; see rust-moderation-anti-cheat and rust-server-permissions-rcon [4].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Measure with the profiler before changing convars

- **Guidance:** Diagnose lag with `fps`, `perf` and a profiler snapshot, then change one setting at a time; remove `-enableProfiler` afterwards.
- **Evidence basis:** Facepunch documents these tools and their costs [2][3], and convar values elsewhere are disputed [10][11][12].
- **Confidence:** High. The tools and warnings are first-party documentation.
- **So what:** You find the actual cost instead of applying unverified hosting-guide numbers.

## Guidance 2 — Size for the wipe peak, not wipe day

- **Guidance:** Treat 12 GB RAM and 15 GB SSD as a floor and add headroom for a 6k map, high population or plugins, watching RAM with `perf 3`.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki says the values are not fixed and that 6k maps use more [1]; `perf 3` shows RAM [3]; one provider says usage rises through a wipe [13].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The floor is first-party, but growth through a wipe is provider experience.
- **So what:** A server that is fine on wipe day can run short later in the wipe.

## Guidance 3 — Prefer a fast per-core CPU

- **Guidance:** Choose high single-thread speed over core count, while knowing parts of the server are now threaded.
- **Evidence basis:** Facepunch gives no CPU figure but documents threaded jobs and networking [1][4][6]; two providers say single-thread speed matters most [10][13].
- **Confidence:** Low. The CPU claim is provider opinion and threading has been changing.
- **So what:** Benchmark your own host rather than buying cores.

## Guidance 4 — Keep UsePlayerUpdateJobs at its default unless testing

- **Guidance:** Leave `UsePlayerUpdateJobs` at 2 and try levels 3 or 4 only on a test server.
- **Evidence basis:** Level 2 is the default and 3 and 4 are labelled experimental [4][5][6].
- **Confidence:** High. Facepunch labels the levels itself.
- **So what:** Experimental levels trade a small frame-time gain for stability risk.

## Guidance 5 — Treat tick, GC and save-interval advice as unverified

- **Guidance:** Verify any `server.tickrate`, `gc.*` or `server.saveinterval` change on a test server with `find` and `fps` before production.
- **Evidence basis:** No Facepunch page opened documents them, and providers conflict [10][11][12].
- **Confidence:** Low. The sources are one class and conflict.
- **So what:** You avoid a change that has no measured effect or that a later build ignores.
title: Rust Server Performance

text:
- No Facepunch page opened documents `server.tickrate`, `gc.buffer` (or `gc.buffercount`, `gc.interval`, `gc.incremental`) or `server.saveinterval`; names, defaults and effects are practitioner-only. Resolve with `find` on a live Livestock server.
- `server.saveinterval` default is 300 per two guides [11][12]; a search snippet from another provider said 600 but that page could not be opened, so it is unresolved.
- `fps.limit` default (30 per [11]) is unconfirmed first-party.
- No official entity-count limit or per-player RAM formula was found.
- Facepunch gives no CPU guidance; the single-thread claim is practitioner-only.
- Industrial default values are from the 2023 build and need re-checking on the October 2026 build.

text:
This deep-dive goes below the administration foundation on three linked topics: who may run admin commands (auth levels 2 and 1 and the commands that grant them), how remote administration works (RCON, its three launch settings, and the Facepunch websocket client), and how the Rust+ companion server is configured. It does not repeat install, wipe or ban material.

Confidence is Medium. The auth-level commands, RCON setting descriptions and the companion-server page are Facepunch wiki pages and are primary. Two things are weaker: the wiki has no dedicated RCON page, and the April 2026 RCON and Rust+ connection-limit convars are named only in general terms in the devblog. The foundation's open question on the `rcon.port` default is resolved here by two consistent primary statements, but with an inference flagged below. Checked against the October 2026 update [6].
title: Rust Server Permissions and RCON

text:
- `ownerid` grants auth level 2 (highest) and `moderatorid` grants level 1; `removeowner` and `removemoderator` revoke them, and the player must reconnect to receive a change [1][2].
- Admin identities persist in `users.cfg` in the server identity `cfg` folder, edited only while the server is shut down [1].
- `rcon.port` is TCP, `rcon.password` is the shared secret (the wiki says "Change this value!!!"), and `rcon.web` selects the connection method, with the wiki suggesting 1 [1].
- Facepunch's README says web RCON (websocket) is intended to become the default and the old RCON to be removed [5].
- Open question resolved (with inference): the wiki says `rcon.port` defaults to the value of `server.port` (28015) [1], and the companion-server page's default of 28082 is consistent only with an RCON default of 28015 [3] *(assessed inference)*.
- The Rust+ companion port defaults to the higher of game port or RCON port plus 67 (28082 with defaults), must be at least 10000, and `app.port` of -1 (written `+app.port 1-`) disables Rust+ [3].
- Spring Clean (April 2026) added RCON and Rust+ connection-limit convars; Livestock (October 2026) fixed one RCON disconnect dropping other RCON connections [4][6].
title: Rust Server Permissions and RCON

text: Covers vanilla dedicated servers on PC: auth levels and the commands that manage them, RCON configuration and security posture, the websocket client, and the Rust+ companion server's settings. Not covered: plugin permission systems such as Oxide or Carbon groups (see rust-modding-plugins-foundation and rust-carbon-vs-oxide), bans and anti-cheat (rust-moderation-anti-cheat), install and ports in general (rust-server-administration-foundation), the full convar catalogue (rust-server-convars-reference) and console editions.
title: Rust Server Permissions and RCON

text:
- **Auth level** — admin tier: 2 owner, 1 moderator [2].
- **RCON** — remote console over the network, configured by `rcon.port`, `rcon.password` and `rcon.web` [1].
- **WebRCON** — the websocket form of RCON, enabled with `+rcon.web 1`, with an open-source browser client from Facepunch [5].
- **Companion server** — the server-side endpoint the Rust+ phone app talks to [3].
- **companion.id** — a file holding the server's identity to Rust+ [3].
title: Rust Server Permissions and RCON

text:
**Granting and revoking levels.** From the server console (or through RCON), run `users` to find a Steam64 ID, then `ownerid <id> "<name>"` or `moderatorid <id> "<name>"`. The wiki says changes save automatically and the player must reconnect to get the level [1]. `ownerid` makes the player "the highest admin auth level (2)", `moderatorid` the "second highest admin auth level (1)", and `removeowner` and `removemoderator` remove them; all four require admin themselves [2]. For file-based management, `users.cfg` sits in `rust/server/server.identity/cfg/`, one line per admin in the form `ownerid 76561198123456789 "TomSmith" ""`, edited only with the server shut down [1].

**RCON.** The wiki describes three launch settings. `rcon.port` is the port RCON clients connect to for admin control and uses TCP. `rcon.password` sets the remote administration password and carries the warning "Change this value!!!". `rcon.web` sets the remote connect method and the page suggests 1 [1]. Facepunch's `webrcon` project describes itself as game server RCON "using websockets"; for Rust, add `+rcon.web 1` and `+rcon.password <password>` to the launch command [5]. The client runs entirely in the browser with no backend, and saved passwords stay in the browser [5].

**Default port reasoning.** The wiki states `rcon.port` defaults to the same value as `server.port`, and gives 28015 as the `server.port` default [1]. The companion server page states its default is the game port plus 67 or the RCON port plus 67, whichever is higher, which is 28082 if ports are unchanged [3]. 28015 plus 67 is 28082, so an RCON default of 28016 would have produced 28083; the two pages therefore agree.

**Query port consequence.** `server.queryport` defaults to one more than the higher of `server.port` or `rcon.port` [1]. With both at 28015 that formula gives 28016, not the 28017 the foundation's table originally gave; the foundation was corrected to 28016 in v1.0.1.

**Rust+ companion server.** `app.info` shows the port and connection settings in use. `app.port` sets the listening port, must be 10000 or higher, and needs a restart. `app.listenip` selects the network interface in complex setups and `app.publicip` overrides the address the app connects to. The TCP port must be reachable from the internet and the server must reach companion-rust.facepunch.com for registration and push notifications [3]. At start-up the server runs a connectivity test; on failure it logs "Rust+ companion server connectivity test failed! Disabling Rust+ features." The test is rate limited to 10 checks per IP every 5 minutes [3]. Rust+ is disabled with `app.port` set to -1, written `+app.port 1-` on the command line because of parser conflicts [3].

**companion.id.** The file is the server's identity to Rust+. It should be kept with backups, never shared, reused on another server or deleted; deleting it generates a new identity that cannot be recovered, and breaking these rules can disable notifications and force players to re-pair [3].
