text:
## Guidance 1 — Grant owner level sparingly and prefer moderator for staff

- **Guidance:** Give level 2 only to the people who must run every command and use level 1 for routine staff.
- **Evidence basis:** The two levels and their revoke commands are documented [2]; the wiki sets no further tiers [1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The levels are documented, but which commands each level can use is not stated on the pages read, so the least-privilege reasoning is inference.
- **So what:** Fewer owner accounts means fewer accounts whose compromise hands over the server.

## Guidance 2 — Treat the RCON password as a root credential and use WebRCON deliberately

- **Guidance:** Set a long, unique `rcon.password` before first launch, use `+rcon.web 1`, and restrict who can reach the RCON TCP port at the firewall.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki warns to change the password and calls the port TCP [1]; Facepunch intends websocket RCON to replace the old protocol [5]; admin commands can be run through RCON [1][2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The facts are primary but the firewall advice is judgement and the pages say nothing about transport encryption.
- **So what:** An exposed RCON port with a weak password gives an attacker full admin.

## Guidance 3 — Decide on Rust+ explicitly instead of leaving it half-working

- **Guidance:** Either open a TCP companion port of 10000 or higher and keep `companion.id` in backups, or disable Rust+ with `+app.port 1-`.
- **Evidence basis:** Failing the connectivity test disables Rust+ anyway and the identity file rules are listed [3].
- **Confidence:** High. Both options are described on the Facepunch page.
- **So what:** A deliberate choice avoids log errors, re-pairing and wasted ports.
title: Rust Server Permissions and RCON

title: Rust Wipes and Map Generation

text:
This deep-dive goes below the overview in the server administration foundation. It covers how a Rust server wipe works at file level (map, blueprint and full wipes), the wipe timer and its schedule tags, the three inputs that define a procedural map (level, seed, world size), the JSON procedural-generation configuration, and how to host and change a custom map.

Confidence is Medium. Nearly every statement rests on Facepunch wiki pages, which are primary, but several pages are marked unfinished, the wiki states no defaults for world size or seed, and the wiki says nothing explicit about a "full wipe" procedure or a forced-wipe calendar date. Those gaps are listed under Open Questions. Checked against the October 2026 update [1].
title: Rust Wipes and Map Generation

text:
- A map wipe happens when the `.sav` file is replaced; a blueprint wipe additionally needs `player.blueprints` deleted [2].
- A forced wipe raises the protocol number in the save file name, so the server starts a new file [2].
- The wipe timer default is the first Thursday of each month at 19:00 Europe/London, which the wiki says aligns with forced wipes [3].
- Schedule tags `monthly`, `biweekly` and `weekly` are mutually exclusive within their group [4].
- A procedural map is defined by size (1000 to 6000), seed (0 to 2147483647) and map type; its file is `.map` named MapType.Size.Seed.map [5][6].
- Procedural-generation JSON settings apply only when a map is first generated; delete the `.map` file to regenerate [7].
- A custom map is served from `+server.levelurl`, which needs a direct, always-available download link [8].
- Facepunch provides no map editor; RustEdit and Rust Map Editor are community tools [9].
title: Rust Wipes and Map Generation

text: Covers vanilla dedicated servers on PC: wipe mechanics and timing, world size and seed, procedural generation customisation, and custom map hosting, against the October 2026 build. Not covered: the full convar list (rust-server-convars-reference), what is on a map (rust-monuments-loot), plugin-driven wipe automation (rust-plugin-development-hooks), and patch history (rust-update-timeline-2026). Console editions are excluded. Building custom maps in an editor is described only at the level of what the wiki documents.
title: Rust Wipes and Map Generation

text:
- **Map wipe** — replacing the `.sav` file so entities, buildings and deployables reset [2].
- **Blueprint (BP) wipe** — deleting `player.blueprints` so learned blueprints reset [2].
- **Forced wipe** — the wipe a new protocol version causes by changing the save file name [2].
- **Protocol number** — the number before a save file's extension [2].
- **Procedural map** — a map generated from size and seed rather than loaded from a file [6].
- **Custom map** — a pre-built `.map` file downloaded from a URL [6][8].
- **Tier / topology** — map terrain classification referenced by the procedural-generation percentages [7].
title: Rust Wipes and Map Generation

text:
**Wipe types at file level.** The `.sav` file holds map data, entities, player buildings and deployables, should share the map's name, and is backed up on each save. Forced wipes generally affect the `.sav` file because they only force a map wipe. To force a blueprint wipe, `player.blueprints` must also be deleted at the same time [2]. The wiki calls it "dangerous and ill-advised to just rename an old sav" to avoid a forced wipe [2]. The wiki does not define a separate "full wipe"; the combination of a new `.sav` and deleted `player.blueprints` is the closest documented equivalent *(assessed reading of [2])*.

**Other persistent files.** `player.deaths` stores death information, `player.states` stores death markers and the hostile timer, `player.tokens` stores per-player Rust+ pairing tokens (removing it forces re-pairing) and `sv.files` stores player signs and contact-system pictures. The page does not say which of these a wipe resets [2].

**Wipe timer.** The timer is configured by `wipetimer.wipeDayofWeek` (0 Sunday to 6 Saturday, default 4), `wipetimer.wipeHourofDay` (default 19, decimals allowed), `wipetimer.wipeTimezone` (default Europe/London), `wipetimer.wipeUnixTimestampOverride` (exact time, overrides everything, ignored if in the past) and `wipetimer.wipeCronOverride` (custom cron expression). `PrintWipe` shows frequency, timezone, wipe time, time remaining and the next 10 occurrences [3].

**Schedule tags.** The wipe schedule group has three tags: monthly (`m`), biweekly (`b`) and weekly (`w`); tags within a group must not be combined [4]. Per the wipe timer page, monthly is the first Thursday of the month, weekly is every Thursday, and biweekly is the first and third Thursday, with a three-week gap in five-week months split into two plus one weeks, all at 19:00 London time [3]. The server-browser tag page lists no blueprint-wipe or map-size tags [4].

**Endgame events.** Events begin on the last day of the wipe cycle, 24 hours before the wipe by default; `eventschedulewipeoffset.event_hours_before_wipe` changes this and 0 disables them. They are the F-15E Strike Eagle flyover (no direct gameplay impact per the wiki) and Road Bradleys, whose count is WorldSize / 1000 * 2 [3].

**Level, seed and size.** `server.level "Procedural Map"` is the only map type the wiki documents; `server.seed` accepts 0 to 2147483647; `server.worldsize` is suggested at 1000 to 6000, and larger maps need more disk and memory [5]. The Map Data page gives the same ranges [6]. Generated maps are stored as `.map` files named MapType.Size.Seed.map in the `maps` folder [6]; the Getting Started page gives the procedural form `proceduralmap.SIZE.SEED.map` [2].

**Procedural generation customisation.** A JSON file in the `server.identity` folder is loaded with `+world.configfile "myConfig.txt"`. Settings apply only when a map is first generated. The four biome percentages are normalised to total 100 percent. Too little Tier0 topology can leave no spawn points, which kicks players for an InsideTerrain violation, and some monuments need specific tiers or biomes and may stop spawning. `Powerlines` does not cover small telephone poles along roads. `AboveGroundRails` only works on maps of size 4250. Use a prefab blacklist or whitelist, not both; matching is by substring [7].

**Custom maps.** Set `+server.levelurl [url]` and remove `+server.worldsize` and `+server.seed`. The host must be up 24/7 because players download from it, the link must be a direct download, and a `file:///` path works only for local testing [8]. Map data changes go through the Rust.World SDK [10]. Facepunch provides no map editor; RustEdit (community, some tools Patreon-gated) and Rust Map Editor (open-source, built on Unity) are community-made [9].

**Changing a custom map mid-wipe.** Shut the server down, change `server.levelurl`, rename the existing `.sav` to match the new map name (for example `MapVersion1.182.sav` to `MapVersion2.182.sav`), and leave the old `.map` in place. Terrain changes can leave trees, nodes and bases floating or buried, and entities added only in the second map do not load [11].

text:
Checked against the October 2026 update [1]. Defaults are as printed on the cited wiki pages.

| Setting | Default / range | Source |
|---------|-----------------|--------|
| `wipetimer.wipeDayofWeek` | 4 (Thursday); 0 to 6 | [3] |
| `wipetimer.wipeHourofDay` | 19; decimals allowed | [3] |
| `wipetimer.wipeTimezone` | Europe/London | [3] |
| `eventschedulewipeoffset.event_hours_before_wipe` | wiki says "within a hour" of the last day; 0 disables | [3] |
| `server.seed` | 0 to 2147483647 (default not stated) | [5] |
| `server.worldsize` | 1000 to 6000 suggested (default not stated) | [5] |
| WorldData `size` field default | 4500 (terrain size in Unity metres) | [6] |
| World serialization number | 10 | [6] |

Procedural-generation JSON defaults, as listed on the wiki [7]:

| Key | Default |
|-----|---------|
| PercentageTier0 / Tier1 / Tier2 | 0.3 / 0.3 / 0.4 |
| PercentageBiomeArid | 0.4 |
| PercentageBiomeTemperate | 0.15 |
| PercentageBiomeTundra | 0.15 |
| PercentageBiomeArctic | 0.3 |
| PercentageBiomeJungle | 0.5 |
| MainRoads, SideRoads, Trails, Rivers, Powerlines | true |
| AboveGroundRails, BelowGroundRails, UnderwaterLabs | true |
| PrefabBlacklist, PrefabWhitelist | empty |

The wiki notes that Jungle replaces 50 percent of the tier 0 biome and that its default was recently lowered and may change again [7]. The wiki example `{ "Trails": false, "PrefabBlacklist": [ "electrical_box_", "powerline_poles" ] }` removes trails and blocks matching prefabs, and a longer example approximates retired barren maps; blacklisting dynamic objects such as bushes causes constant console spam [7].

Custom-map hosting convars for maps without an ocean: `baseboat.generate_paths false` and `cargoship.event_enabled false`, plus optionally `ai.ocean_patrol_path_iterations 0` (static cargo ship) [11].

A mandatory server and client update is set for 22 October at 18:00 BST [1].

text:
- Editing the procedural-generation JSON and expecting an existing map to change; delete the `.map` file first [7].
- Lowering Tier0 too far, causing spawn-less terrain and InsideTerrain kicks [7].
- Reusing a filename for an updated custom map, which makes clients load the cached copy and show "World cache version mismatch" or "World File Outdated" [11].
- Hosting the map behind a page with a click-through button, a Discord message link, or a Dropbox link without `dl=1`; none give a direct download [8][11].
- Renaming an old `.sav` to dodge a forced wipe [2].
- Running a custom map with no accessible ocean, which can freeze loading until the cargo ship event is disabled [11].
- Expecting `AboveGroundRails` to take effect on a non-4250 map [7].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Treat the default wipe timer as correct and change cadence by tag, not by hacking files

- **Guidance:** Keep the default timer and pick monthly, biweekly or weekly as the browser tag; use the override convars only for deliberate off-cycle wipes.
- **Evidence basis:** The wiki says the default aligns with forced wipes [3], tags are mutually exclusive [4], and renaming saves is discouraged [2].
- **Confidence:** High. All three statements are first-party Facepunch wiki text.
- **So what:** A schedule that matches the tag you advertise avoids player confusion and broken saves.

## Guidance 2 — Decide blueprint wipe policy explicitly at each wipe

- **Guidance:** Write down per wipe whether you delete `player.blueprints`, because a forced wipe alone does not reset blueprints.
- **Evidence basis:** Forced wipes generally affect only the `.sav`; a BP wipe needs the extra deletion [2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The mechanic is documented, but the wiki gives no BP-wipe tag, so how players learn your policy is inference.
- **So what:** State the policy in the server description to avoid disputes.

## Guidance 3 — Generate and inspect the map before opening the server

- **Guidance:** Test a seed and world size on a private instance, then lock them; change procedural JSON only before first generation.
- **Evidence basis:** Config applies only at first generation [7], size affects resource needs [5], and overly sparse Tier0 can break spawning [7].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The constraints are documented; the advice to preview is a practice recommendation.
- **So what:** Avoids a mid-wipe regenerate that would force a wipe.

## Guidance 4 — Version every custom map file name and plan for no mid-wipe terrain edits

- **Guidance:** Use a new unique filename per map version, host on infrastructure you control, and avoid swapping maps mid-wipe.
- **Evidence basis:** Same-name caching causes client mismatch errors [11]; mid-wipe swaps leave floating objects and skip new entities [11]; the host must be always available [8].
- **Confidence:** High. Facepunch's FAQ documents each failure directly.
- **So what:** Fewer connection failures and no corrupted bases.
title: Rust Wipes and Map Generation

- The wiki gives no defaults for `server.worldsize` and `server.seed`; verify on a running server. The WorldData default of 4500 is a file-format field, not necessarily the server default [6].

title: Rust Game Modes and Server Types

text:
Rust servers differ along three independent axes: the game mode set by `server.gamemode` (vanilla, softcore, hardcore, primitive, plus test and placeholder modes), the wipe schedule (weekly, biweekly, monthly), and who runs the server (Facepunch or a community operator, with or without Oxide or Carbon). The Facepunch wiki lists the modes and the server browser tag groups; Facepunch devblogs from 2021, 2022, 2025 and July 2026 describe what each mode actually changes [1][2][3][4][5][6].

This answers the foundation's open question about modes beyond softcore and hardcore: the wiki lists primitive and weapontest, and the February 2025 devblog documents Primitive in detail [1][6]. Document confidence is Medium. Mode rules come from primary sources but from posts of different ages, and the current official availability of each mode could not be confirmed.
title: Rust Game Modes and Server Types

text:
- The wiki lists these working modes: vanilla, survival (same as vanilla), softcore, hardcore, weapontest and primitive; deathmatch, teamdm, onedeath, koth_solo and koth_team are marked "Placeholder: not working currently" [1].
- Server browser tags have mutually exclusive groups for wipe schedule (monthly, biweekly, weekly) and difficulty (vanilla, hardcore, softcore) [2].
- Default wipe schedules are monthly (first Thursday), weekly (every Thursday) and biweekly (first and third Thursday), all at 19:00 London time [7].
- Softcore in the Common Ground update (2 Jul 2026) has a 2x gather multiplier and default raid windows of 6 PM to 9 PM server time [5].
- Hardcore (August 2025 rules) hides the map without a compass, forbids crafting and researching firearms, multiplies ammo crafting cost by 5 and doubles upkeep [3].
- Facepunch's server guidelines allow community servers but forbid calling them "official" [8].
- Facepunch said in 2025 that such modes are not expected to stay popular for long, "usually just a couple of months" [3].

title: Rust Game Modes and Server Types

text:
- **Game mode:** the ruleset selected with `server.gamemode` at startup or `gamemode.set` at runtime [1].
- **Vanilla:** the default Rust ruleset; also a tag in the difficulty group [1][2].
- **Raid window:** in softcore, the daily period in which raiding is unrestricted [5].
- **Reclaim terminal:** softcore safezone terminal from which part of a dead player's inventory is recovered [1][4].
- **Server browser tag:** a short code in the server's tag list that the browser filters on [2].
title: Rust Game Modes and Server Types

text:
**Selecting a mode.** `server.gamemode <name>` sets the mode in the startup config and `gamemode.set <name>` sets it at runtime. The wiki warns not to switch modes mid-wipe, because this resets all players and their inventory [1].

**Vanilla.** The wiki describes vanilla as "Default Rust gameplay" and says not to set it explicitly; survival is the same ruleset under a different label [1]. The 2021 and 2022 devblogs both state that most servers remained regular vanilla Rust [4][9].

**Softcore.** Described by the wiki as "Vanilla gameplay but with some changes to make the game easier" [1]. At launch (4 Feb 2021): half of a dead player's inventory is recoverable at the death spot or a reclaim terminal at Bandit Town or the Outpost, reclaim items despawn after 2 hours, all players can spawn at either safezone, only a wounded player's contents may be viewed, and maximum team size is 4 [4]. Wiki convars set reclaim fractions: belt 0.5, main 0.5, wear 0 by default [1]. The Common Ground update (2 Jul 2026) added a 2x resource gather multiplier, raid windows (default 6 PM to 9 PM server time, same zone for everyone), and Tool Cupboard raid blocking outside windows, where a cupboard must be at least 1 hour old to block raids. Building blocks and doors cannot be raided outside the window, but deployables and unprotected cupboards can still be attacked. Owners received convars to tune this [5].

**Hardcore.** The wiki describes it as vanilla "with lots of features disabled or limited" [1]. The original post (26 Aug 2022) removed contact system, compass, crawling, global chat, Rust+, team system, map, MLRS and safe zones; added 100 m local chat and a limit of 5 sleeping bags and beds; made blueprints wipe monthly; and launched 10 official servers [9]. The "Harder Core" post (August 2025) said hardcore was returning with changes: fog of war on the map, map position hidden unless a compass is on the belt, firearms cannot be crafted or researched (found weapons can be repaired), ammunition crafting costs up 5x, respawn cooldowns of 15 minutes (sleeping bags) and 10 minutes (beds), and doubled upkeep [3]. The compass item exists in all modes, but the map and UI changes apply only to hardcore [3]. The clan system is disabled in hardcore [5].

**Primitive.** Released with the February 2025 update (article dated 6 Feb 2025), framed as high-tech knowledge being lost. It removes rockets, C4 and the MLRS, metal and armoured building grades and armoured doors, the facemask and metal chest plate, four monuments (Oil Rig, Missile Silo, Excavator, Underwater Labs), the underground train, Scientist NPCs (vendors remain), the patrol helicopter, cargo ship and Bradley events, and the minicopter, scrap transport helicopter and attack helicopter. Sulfur nodes spawn at half rate, tech tree tax is doubled, and wild horse spawns are doubled [6].

**Other modes.** Weapontest is "For test purposes. Made for testing weapon changes" [1].

**Wipe schedule tags.** Monthly, biweekly and weekly are server browser tags; the wiki defines their default times [2][7]. A host can override the day, hour, timezone, a Unix timestamp or a cron expression [7].

**Type tags.** Beyond difficulty, the browser has type tags: pve, roleplay, creative, minigame, training (combat training), battlefield, broyale (battle royale), builds, tut (tutorial) and premium; modding tags are modded, Oxide and Carbon; regions are NA, SA, EU, WA, EA, OC and AF. The wiki advises against several tags from the same group on one server because searches may fail to match [2].

**Official versus community.** Facepunch lets anyone run private, unofficial or community servers, allows monetisation, and instructs operators not to call a server "official" [8]. The 2025 browser changes describe horizontal Play tab server-type tabs starting at "Official", sorting by mode and showing queue sizes [3]. Servers must meet a minimum encryption level to be treated as secure, and insecure servers need the `-insecure` startup parameter [10].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Read the server's tags and description before assuming any rules

- **Guidance:** Check the difficulty, wipe and modding tags, then the server description, before applying guide numbers to a server.
- **Evidence basis:** Tag groups [2]; mode differences [3][5][6]; softcore multiplier matching modded servers [5].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The tags and modes are documented, but tags are self-declared by operators.
- **So what:** A "vanilla" tagged server may still run plugins, and rates can differ from this KB's vanilla values.

## Guidance 2 — Admins should pick a mode at wipe start and tag accurately

- **Guidance:** Set `server.gamemode` before the first wipe boot, use one tag per group, and avoid "official" in naming.
- **Evidence basis:** Mid-wipe switch warning [1]; tag advice [2]; server guidelines [8].
- **Confidence:** High. All three come directly from Facepunch pages.
- **So what:** Avoids player resets, missed browser matches and delisting risk.

## Guidance 3 — Treat Hardcore and Primitive as temporary experiments

- **Guidance:** Do not plan a long-lived community around a Facepunch experimental mode without a fallback to vanilla.
- **Evidence basis:** "A couple of months" statement and shutdown note [3][1].
- **Confidence:** Medium. It is an inference from Facepunch's stated expectation and one wiki note.
- **So what:** Expect rule changes or removal; recheck the devblog monthly.

title: Rust Skins and Cosmetics

text:
This document explains how Rust skins and cosmetics reach players: community creators build skins with the Steam Workshop tooling, Facepunch selects some for the game, and players obtain them through crates, the Steam marketplace, the Steam item store, the in-game store and DLC packs. It also records what Facepunch has said about skins being cosmetic, and the server-hosting guidelines on paid content. It gives no price or investment advice.

Document-level confidence is Medium. The founding statements and the current server guidelines are first-party Facepunch sources, but the key policy statements on cosmetic-only skins date from 2015, and no single current Facepunch page defines the cosmetic-only rule. Prices, rarity, and the store's current catalogue were deliberately not collected.
title: Rust Skins and Cosmetics

text:
- In a 20 August 2015 devblog Facepunch said of Workshop skins: "these are just skins, they don't offer any differing properties" [1].
- In July 2015 Facepunch said "The items we're adding are cosmetic, and we're not charging for them" about its first inventory items, which were awarded by playtime [2].
- Skins are made by community creators through the Steam Workshop; since October 2016 an integrated in-game workshop publishes to Steam on "Publish" [3][4].
- Creators must accept the Contributor Agreement before items can be visible or added to the game; Facepunch weighs quality, community votes and presentation [5].
- A permanent in-game store launched on 18 November 2021; its items cannot be traded on Steam or resold on the Steam Community Market [6].
- The Facepunch server guidelines (last updated 15 July 2025) forbid granting Facepunch DLC to players who have not validly purchased it, and forbid bypassing ownership checks [7].
- The October 2026 update added a Plague Doctor Hazmat Suit DLC and made all ladder hatches Workshop-skinnable [8].
title: Rust Skins and Cosmetics

text: Covers PC Rust (Steam): how skins are created and selected, how players obtain cosmetics, what Facepunch has said about cosmetic-only status, and the server-side policy on cosmetic and DLC content. Build checked: October 2026 update. Excludes prices, market values, trading advice, console editions, and the full current catalogue of skins and DLC packs.
title: Rust Skins and Cosmetics

text:
- **Skin:** an alternate appearance for an existing item or deployable. In 2015 Facepunch described Workshop skins as having no "differing properties" [1].
- **Workshop skinnable:** an item that the Workshop tooling lets creators reskin; the October 2026 update added all ladder hatches [8].
- **Facepunch DLC:** per the server guidelines, paid content packs such as building skins, decor packs, hazmat skins and instruments, plus approved in-game purchases [7].
- **Contributor Agreement:** the agreement a creator must accept before items become publicly visible or eligible for the game [5].
title: Rust Skins and Cosmetics

text:
**Creation.** In July 2015 the Workshop SDK let players create skins, initially limited to t-shirts and trousers, and Facepunch said items would go in if they were not "a terrible meme, someone else's IP" and fit Rust's style [3]. By August 2015 jackets, a snow jacket, a boonie hat and a balaclava were also skinnable [1]. In October 2016 an integrated in-game workshop let creators edit skins in-game; clicking "Publish" generated an icon and uploaded to the Steam Workshop [4].

**Selection.** The Workshop FAQ says creators must accept the Contributor Agreement; when two submissions are similar, the team considers overall quality, community votes and presentation; creators without a prior approved item may get priority; and community conduct can affect decisions [5]. The Facepunch wiki guidance says items should "look dirty and worn", skins must stay within the tier of the item (a burlap item that looks like metal may be rejected as it could be mistaken for armour), text lowers the chance of acceptance, and items with few skins are good targets [9]. That wiki page is marked as last updated "A Long Time Ago" [9].

**Obtaining.** The Workshop FAQ says players get skins by crafting crates from items in their inventory or by buying items on the marketplace, that skins are released in limited runs, and that they are removed from the store after a long time on sale or after earning enough revenue and may then appear in crates [5]. Artists do not receive money from crates or the marketplace, and the team does not sell crates directly [5]. In August 2015 Facepunch said players must unlock Workshop items in game before crafting them [1]. A 2021 launch post describes a permanent store selling premium cosmetics and skins year round [6]. The October 2026 update says the Plague Doctor Hazmat Suit "can be purchased in-game or from the Rust Steam item store" [8].

**Store trading rules.** Items from the permanent store cannot be traded on Steam or resold on the Steam Community Market and "hold no resale monetary value"; Facepunch said this was to differentiate them from earlier items and that it would keep the policy under review [6].

**Cosmetic-only statement.** The August 2015 devblog says Workshop skins are "just skins, they don't offer any differing properties" and advises "If you're in any kind of doubt - don't buy them, they're just cosmetics" [1]. The wiki rule against skins resembling higher-tier items exists because they could be mistaken for armour [9].

**Server-side.** The guidelines require servers to give unrestricted access to validly purchased Facepunch DLC, and forbid granting DLC to non-owners, bypassing ownership checks or artificially enabling DLC; test servers may temporarily restrict or grant DLC for testing only [7]. Servers may restrict custom or Steam Workshop content that Facepunch does not sell or gate, may charge a single fee or subscription, and may sell cosmetic items, effects or enhancements [7].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Treat skins as appearance only, but check clothing separately

- **Guidance:** Assume Workshop skins change appearance, not stats, but verify stats for clothing and attire items on the wiki.
- **Evidence basis:** Facepunch's 2015 statement [1]; the wiki Hoodie stats [10]; the tier-matching rule [9].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The statement is first-party but dated 2015, with no current restatement found.
- **So what:** Players can choose skins freely, yet should not assume a differently named clothing item has identical protection.

## Guidance 2 — Server owners should never unlock DLC for non-owners

- **Guidance:** Do not use plugins or settings that grant Facepunch DLC to players who have not bought it; sell only your own cosmetic content.
- **Evidence basis:** Server guidelines on ownership checks and cosmetic sales [7].
- **Confidence:** High. The rule is stated directly in the current first-party guidelines.
- **So what:** Avoid enforcement risk; read the guidelines page again after each revision.

## Guidance 3 — Treat store and trading rules as time-sensitive

- **Guidance:** Re-check the current store and marketplace rules before relying on any trading claim here.
- **Evidence basis:** 2021 store post said policy stays under review [6]; catalogue changes in the latest update [8].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Only the 2021 and 2026 posts were opened.
- **So what:** Do not infer current tradeability from a 2021 post.

title: Rust System Requirements and Platforms

text:
This document records what Facepunch and Double Eleven publish about what hardware and platforms Rust runs on: the Steam store minimum and recommended specifications for Windows and macOS, the stated status of Linux, the TPM and Secure Boot requirement that servers can opt in to, and the console edition as a separate product.

Document-level confidence is Medium. The specifications come from the Steam page and the Facepunch wiki, both first-party, but the Steam page was read through a summarising fetch tool, the wiki page is marked as long out of date, and the TPM and Secure Boot rollout beyond opt-in servers has no dated global requirement in any source opened.
title: Rust System Requirements and Platforms

text:
- The Steam page lists a Windows minimum of Windows 11 64-bit, Ryzen 5 1400 or Core i5-6600, 12 GB RAM, GTX 1060 / RX 470 / Arc A580, DirectX 11 and 45 GB storage [1].
- The recommended Windows spec is Ryzen 7 3700X or i7-6700K, 16 GB RAM, RTX 3060 / RX 6600 XT / Arc B580, DirectX 12, with an SSD required [1].
- macOS minimum and recommended specs are listed separately and require an Apple M1 (recommended M1 Pro, Max or Ultra) and macOS Monterey (12) [1].
- The Steam page lists no Linux requirements, and the Facepunch wiki says the game is not natively supported on Linux [1][2].
- Servers can require TPM and Secure Boot; as of Spring Clean (2 Apr 2026) Facepunch said only about 60% of players had the features enabled [3][4].
- Facepunch states its end goal is to make the requirement global, with no date given [3][5].
- Rust Console Edition is developed and published by Double Eleven for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, with no cross-platform progress transfer [6].

text:
- **TPM 2.0:** a hardware or firmware security module; Facepunch's devblogs refer to "TPM and Secure Boot" and "TPM 2.0" [3][4].
- **Secure Boot:** a firmware setting; Facepunch describes the requirement as applying to Windows PCs [3].
- **Secure tag:** server-browser tag shown on servers that require TPM and Secure Boot for every player [3].
- **Console Edition:** the PS5 and Xbox Series X|S version, developed and published by Double Eleven [6].
title: Rust System Requirements and Platforms

text:
**PC specification.** The Steam page lists separate Windows and macOS requirement blocks. Windows is "64-bit processor and operating system" required, with an SSD "highly recommended" at minimum and "required" at recommended [1]. The Facepunch wiki's installation page repeats the same Windows figures and recommends verifying game files through Steam if files are corrupt [2].

**Operating systems.** The Steam page lists Windows and macOS requirement tabs and no Linux tab [1]. The wiki states "Rust is currently available for Windows and macOS" and "The game is not natively supported on Linux at this time" [2]. Rust is sold exclusively through Steam per the wiki [2]. The Steam page also states the game uses kernel-level anti-cheat (Easy Anti-Cheat) and needs agreement to a third-party EULA [1].

**TPM and Secure Boot.** The Shipshape devblog (5 Mar 2026) introduced the option for servers to require TPM and Secure Boot; a server-wide convar enforces it for everyone and earns the Secure tag, while a per-player convar does not add the tag [3]. The post gave adoption as over 80% with TPM hardware and just under 60% with Secure Boot enabled, said players can check compatibility with Windows commands, and said hardware from roughly the last eight years is likely to support it [3]. Spring Clean reported about 1 cheater per 63 players on the six secure servers against 1 per 42 on regular servers, and about 60% of players with the features enabled, and said Facepunch did not want to alienate players [4]. Livestock (1 Oct 2026) said servers were introduced in March, strongly recommended enabling the features if hardware supports them, and described a reduced cheater presence [5]. Only Windows is discussed; the posts say nothing about Linux or Mac [3][5].

**Console edition.** Double Eleven's FAQ says the edition is available for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, is published and developed by Double Eleven, has no physical copies, and does not support cross-platform progress transfer [6]. Its wipe schedule is separate from PC: weekly servers wipe Thursdays 6 PM UTC and monthly servers on the last Thursday of the month at 6 PM UTC [6].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Check TPM and Secure Boot before joining secure-tagged servers

- **Guidance:** Players with supported hardware should enable TPM and Secure Boot, since a share of servers can refuse connections without them.
- **Evidence basis:** Opt-in server enforcement and the Secure tag [3]; Facepunch's strong recommendation to enable [5].
- **Confidence:** High. Stated directly by Facepunch in two devblogs.
- **So what:** Missing firmware settings can lock a player out of secure servers; hardware roughly eight years old or newer is likely to qualify [3].

## Guidance 2 — Treat the minimum spec as a floor and buy to the recommended one

- **Guidance:** Aim for the recommended Windows spec with an SSD for comfortable play.
- **Evidence basis:** Minimum and recommended figures and SSD wording [1][2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The figures are first-party but real performance depends on settings and map, which no source quantifies.
- **So what:** 12 GB RAM and a GTX 1060 class card are the stated floor; expect longer loads without an SSD [1].

## Guidance 3 — Linux players should not rely on official client support

- **Guidance:** Assume no official Linux client support.
- **Evidence basis:** No Linux requirements on Steam and the wiki statement [1][2].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Absence of a listing is inferred, and compatibility-layer behaviour was not investigated.
- **So what:** Players on Linux should expect no first-party help and should check anti-cheat behaviour themselves.

The March, April, May, June, July, August and October devblogs opened for this document do not state a force-wipe date as such; they describe wipe-relative behaviour (for example the Deep Sea not opening right after a wipe [7]).

## Guidance 1 — Expect the next content update on Thursday 5 November 2026, but confirm it

- **Guidance:** Plan for a monthly update on the first Thursday of November (5 November 2026) after the 22 October Halloween Update, and treat the date as unconfirmed until Facepunch posts it.
- **Evidence basis:** Nine consecutive first-Thursday update posts from February to October [1][2]; the stated monthly plan [3]; the announced 22 October Halloween Update [14].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The pattern is solid, but the January post warned some months may be light and Facepunch has not announced November.
- **So what:** Admins schedule mod and wipe preparation for 5 November while watching the news index, and players treat the date as likely rather than guaranteed.

## Guidance 2 — Read experimental toggles as short-lived

- **Guidance:** Do not build long-term server configuration on features flagged experimental or opt-in in a given month.
- **Evidence basis:** Jobs levels moved from experimental to default within months [9][11][12]; the Rust Render Pipeline toggle is stated to last the first month [14]; the navmesh was opt-in in June and still being tested in September [10][13].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The pattern is documented across several posts, but whether each feature ships is unknown.
- **So what:** Re-check the devblog each month before relying on an experimental convar.

text:
This document explains how Rust ships updates: a major content update on the first Thursday of each month, announced by a Facepunch devblog, with the official force wipe tied to that release. It covers how to read a devblog, which Steam branches exist for testing, how game modes such as softcore differ from vanilla, platform and licence facts, and a timeline of the eight most recent monthly updates (March to October 2026) read directly from Facepunch.

Document-level confidence is Medium. The monthly cadence and the devblog contents are directly verified from primary Facepunch sources. The exact force-wipe hour, the console edition's current schedule, and the purpose of non-staging branches rest on a community wiki, secondary reporting, or could not be confirmed.
title: Rust Updates and Meta: Foundation

text:
- Each of the eight monthly devblogs from March to October 2026 is dated the first Thursday of its month [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9].
- The Facepunch wiki states the default wipe schedules (monthly, weekly, biweekly) "align with force wipes" and gives the monthly default as the first Thursday of the month at 19:00 London time [11].
- The latest verified update is the "Livestock Update" of 1 October 2026 [2]; by the same pattern the next would fall on 5 November 2026 *(assessed)*.
- Server owners can test unreleased builds with SteamCMD `app_update 258550 -beta staging` or `-beta aux01` [12].
- Rust left Early Access on 8 February 2018 and is published by Facepunch Studios on Windows and macOS on Steam [13][14].
- Console editions are a separate product developed with Double Eleven, with PS5 and Xbox Series X/S versions released 26 June 2025 [14].
- None of the eight reviewed devblogs explicitly mentions a force wipe [2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9].

text:
- **Force wipe:** the monthly Facepunch release after which servers are expected to reset map and progress. The wiki treats default wipe schedules as aligned to it [11].
- **Devblog:** the monthly Facepunch news post on rust.facepunch.com describing an update and its changelist [1].
- **Staging / aux01:** optional Steam beta branches for testing unreleased builds [12].
- **Softcore / hardcore:** game modes referenced in the Common Ground update; softcore has a 2x gather multiplier and raid windows [5].
title: Rust Updates and Meta: Foundation

text:
**Cadence.** The Facepunch news index lists a devblog on the first Thursday of every month from March to October 2026 [1]. Wikipedia reports that after leaving Early Access the update cycle moved from weekly to monthly, citing PC Gamer [14]. The Facepunch wiki gives the default monthly wipe as the first Thursday at 19:00 London time and notes defaults align with force wipes [11].

**Reading a devblog.** Posts are titled with a theme name and dated; the page contains headline features, followed by a changelist (the "Breach and Clear" post is labelled the September Update Changelist, and "Power Trip" gives changelist 4044) [3][4]. Convar names and launch parameters appear inline, for example `vehicle.padrepairsrequired` [2], `antihack.parenthistory` [6], and the opt-in `-useNewNavmesh` parameter [3]. Experimental or opt-in features are flagged in the text, such as the Rust Render Pipeline toggle [2]. Wipe-relevant behaviour is usually stated in terms of "the wipe" rather than a dated force wipe [2][6]. Non-update news posts exist and are not devblogs, for example the Lunar New Year post [10].

**Branches.** The Facepunch wiki says beta branches let you test features not released to the public, using SteamCMD against app ID 258550, with `staging` and `aux01` as the documented examples; moving back requires specifying `public` [12]. The "Shipshape" post mentions data from an "EU Staging server" [9]. The purpose of aux01 beyond testing is not stated in the sources opened.

**Modes and server types.** The "Common Ground" update documents Softcore changes (2x resource gather multiplier, scheduled raid windows defaulting to 6 PM to 9 PM server time with Tool Cupboard raid blocking outside them) and notes the clan system is disabled in hardcore mode [5]. The wiki's server page lists a "Gamemodes" topic under server hosting [15]. Community servers set their own wipe timing; the wiki exposes `wipeDayofWeek`, `wipeHourofDay`, `wipeTimezone` and cron overrides for the in-game wipe timer [11].

**Platform and licence.** Steam lists Facepunch Studios as developer and publisher, with a release date of 8 February 2018 and Windows and macOS support [13]. Early Access began December 2013 and ended 8 February 2018 [14]. The Steam page does not state an Early Access status, only a user tag [13]. Console editions for PS4 and Xbox One launched 21 May 2021 with Double Eleven; PS5 and Xbox Series X/S early access began 19 June 2025 with full release 26 June 2025; the PS4/Xbox One versions were delisted 29 May 2025 and their servers shut in October 2025 [14].

text:
## Guidance 1 — Plan around the first Thursday and re-verify details each month

- **Guidance:** Treat the first Thursday of each month as update and wipe day, and recheck the devblog for that month before relying on any value in this knowledge base.
- **Evidence basis:** Eight consecutive devblogs on first Thursdays [1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9]; wiki defaults aligned with force wipes [11].
- **Confidence:** High. The pattern is directly observed in primary sources for eight months and matches the wiki.
- **So what:** Players schedule wipe-day play for the first Thursday; admins plan mod updates the same day.

## Guidance 2 — Admins should pin the branch and expect plugin lag

- **Guidance:** Run the public branch for live servers, use staging or aux01 only on a test server, and delay the wipe-day launch until the framework you use has updated.
- **Evidence basis:** Branch commands and the Oxide reinstall warning [12]; the staging server reference [9].
- **Confidence:** Medium. The commands are documented but the stability of each branch is not stated in the sources opened.
- **So what:** A test server on staging catches plugin breakage before wipe day.

## Guidance 3 — Check the specific mode before quoting rates or rules

- **Guidance:** Do not assume vanilla values apply on softcore or modded servers; verify the mode first.
- **Evidence basis:** Softcore 2x gather and raid windows [5]; wipe timer configurable by hosts [11].
- **Confidence:** Medium. Mode behaviour is documented for softcore only; other modes were not verified.
- **So what:** Guides quoting vanilla numbers can be wrong on community servers.

- Console Edition's current 2026 update and wipe cadence could not be confirmed from an official source; reporting found was dated 2021 to 2022.
